articles.title: Nvidia wants to turn old nuclear power plants into huge AI data centers — but says it draws the line at turning them back on
articles.content: Nvidia wants to turn Germany's retired nuclear sites into AI data centers Germany's nuclear shutdown leaves dozens of former power stations awaiting dismantling Nvidia and PreussenElektra are investigating new uses for Germany's retired nuclear facilities Nvidia has agreed to examine whether shuttered German reactor sites could become computing hubs, though the company rules out restarting any idle units. The US chipmaker signed a preliminary agreement with PreussenElektra GmbH (PEL), a utility from Germany, to study the idea at decommissioned locations. The arrangement does not involve generating electricity from fission for any future facility, since the work concentrates on existing grid links and water access. Reusing sites without reviving reactors Following the Fukushima incident, Germany permanently closed its final operating reactors in April 2023 and is now dismantling about 30 atomic stations nationwide. PreussenElektra oversees the closure and teardown of eight of those stations, and these are probably the locations that will receive scrutiny. Neither company has named the sites under review, so the eight locations managed by PreussenElektra remain an assumption rather than a confirmed list. “Our former power plant sites have valuable industrial infrastructure and offer opportunities for new, future-oriented uses,” said Guido Knott, chairman of PEL’s management board. “Together with NVIDIA, we intend to conduct a sound assessment of whether and how these conditions can be leveraged for AI factories.” The assessment will review grid connections, open land and industrial infrastructure to judge whether each site satisfies the strict operating requirements of AI factories. The two companies say they will test whether the sites can meet engineering and running needs while supporting Germany's computing capacity for AI. Cost savings and an unproven case New data center facilities normally need well-located land, industrial zone approvals, access to water for cooling, and powerful grid connections, which former atomic stations already possess. Nvidia hopes that reusing these locations could lower expenses and shorten development schedules compared with constructing new campuses during an unprecedented expansion of AI infrastructure. “AI factories require access to power, land and high-capacity infrastructure, and former industrial sites could provide a strong foundation for this next generation of computing,” said Markus Hacker, senior regional director at Nvidia. “Together with PreussenElektra, we will assess how its sites could meet the technical and operational requirements of AI factories and contribute to Germany’s high-performance AI infrastructure.” Both companies describe the effort as exploratory, and neither has disclosed funding figures, sanctioned designs or binding building contracts, so the idea remains unproven. Reusing atomic stations looks efficient on paper, yet neither company has shown that grid capacity at the sites matches the power appetite of AI clusters. Approval processes for dismantled facilities, local acceptance and the cost of conversion remain unaddressed, so any savings in time or money are still speculative. The refusal to revive reactors may ease political concerns in Germany, although the announcement does not say whether regional authorities or residents have been consulted. Via Tom's Hardware
articles.author: Efosa Udinmwen

articles.title: Hisense XR10 review: a pricy powerhouse projector with huge dynamic range in both the light and dark
articles.content: Hisense XR10: One-minute review The Hisense XR10 offers powerful projection that you can put all over the room and still get squared away. That’s thanks to extensive optical adjustments that include incredible zoom range and lens shift. Hisense definitely cranked up the elegance this year. The Hisense XR10 is loaded up with blazing RGB lasers that give it stunning brightness and color, while an adjustable iris can help it clamp down black levels for dark room viewing with enhanced contrast. It’s all packed into a stylish box that’s much smaller and more portable than high-end theater projectors like the Sony Bravia Projector 7 , and Hisense’s included carrying case will let you take it places in style. (Image credit: Future) All of this comes at a high price, though. The Hisense XR10 is $5,999 / £5,999 / AU$9,999 after falling from the original $6,999 price tag in the US. Though it has decent speakers for a projector and a serviceable operating system in VidaaOS, these don’t lend a ton of extra value. It also jumped the gun a bit and missed out on the VRR and 4K/120Hz support that a newer wave of projectors are offering. At its price, it’s not going to lead the charge for value, but you do get a lot for the money. It’s still probably worth waiting to see if the XGIMI Horizon 30 Ultra Max, JMGO Iris Ultra Max, and Hisense C3 Ultra Max leave the XR10 any room to breathe. Hisense XR10 review: Price and release date Release date: mid 2026 MSRP: $5,999 / £5,999 / AU$9,999 The Hisense XR10 made its debut at CES 2026 and started shipping in May. It came with an initial price of $6,999 / £5,999 / AU$9,999 but that US price has generally fallen to $5,999. In the time it’s been out, some deals have even brought it as low as $4,499, but it hasn’t been a sticky price drop and prices elsewhere seem to be much more static. For the money, Hisense does include a special carrying case that’s far and away the highest quality one I’ve seen included with a projector like this. But even then it’s not adding thousands of dollars in value. Hisense XR10 review: specs Supported screen sizes 65-300 inches Optical technology 3 Laser DLP Brightness (specified) 6,000 Lumens Audio 2x8-watt + 15-watt speakers Ports 2x HDMI 2.1 (1x eARC), 1x HDMI 2.0, 2x USB-A, 1x optical, 1x 3.5mm audio Smart TV VidaaOS Dimensions 11.5 x 10.7 x 8.4 inches Weight 23.4 pounds Hisense XR10 review: design and features Stylish, compact design and serious carrying case Highly adjustable optics VidaaOS is quick but may be limiting Hisense has built something particularly gorgeous with the XR10. It simply looks like a work of serious engineering with its brown metal casing, stylish venting and machined accents, knurled lens cover, oversize lens cover, and dark color scheme. The front's sensor array also looks highly technical. The top is a little plain, but Hisense has included a volume dial, power button, ambient light sensor, and a little aesthetic nod to the RGB laser system inside. The Hisense XR10 is a modestly sized box at 11.5 x 10.7 x 8.4 inches / 292.1 x 271.8 x 213.4 mm, yet with all its packing in it ends up weighing a considerable 23.4 pounds / 10.6kg. To help you lug it around, Hisense includes a fashionable carrying case that looks more like a piece of luggage than the styrofoam cases many projectors come with. It's complete with straps, zippers, padded slots for each component, and it even has wheels and an extendable handle for rolling. (Image credit: Future) The projector has everything it needs to help you get it set up for perfect alignment with your screen. It stands on four height-adjustable feet, so you can get it level and squared away with the wall. And it offers extensive zoom and lens shift capabilities. It can shift from a short throw ratio of 0.84:1 all the way to a 2:1 throw ratio, this means you can set it close to a wall or screen and still get a big picture or set it far from that screen and shrink it down to fit without having to use digital…

articles.title: New York Knicks slammed after offering employees NBA championship rings in what turned out to be a phishing test
articles.content: Knicks employees expecting free championship rings received mandatory cybersecurity training instead A fake championship ring offer exposed employees to an internal phishing test Madison Square Garden admitted that using championship jewellery as bait was inappropriate The New York Knicks have faced criticism after sending employees an email promising complimentary NBA championship rings that turned out to be a cybersecurity exercise. Staff members who accepted the invitation were reportedly required to complete cybersecurity training instead of receiving jewellery commemorating the franchise's historic victory. The incident involved workers at Madison Square Garden, where expectations of receiving championship memorabilia had already grown following the team's successful season. Fake championship ring offer triggers mandatory training The deceptive message circulated in late September, offering recipients personalized jewellery supposedly manufactured by the same company responsible for producing players' rings. Employees could select between two advertised designs, Championship Gold and Garden Classic, before following a link to register their preferred choice. However, the invitation was actually part of an internal security assessment intended to identify workers susceptible to fraudulent messages and credential theft. Those who followed the instructions were reportedly assigned compulsory cybersecurity lessons, although the organization has not disclosed how many employees were affected. Joe Vardon, a senior NBA journalist at The Athletic , reported that several individuals familiar with the situation verified the exercise's purpose. The report also raised questions about whether the invitation contained recognizable warning signs that might have helped employees identify the deception. Such exercises commonly use suspicious addresses or misleading website links, although the specific indicators included in this particular message remain unknown. The controversy followed the Knicks' first NBA championship since 1973, making the promised jewellery particularly significant for employees celebrating the achievement. Receiving commemorative jewellery was also a reasonable expectation because NBA organizations commonly distribute less expensive versions to personnel outside their playing squads. Madison Square Garden acknowledges its mistake Madison Square Garden Sports subsequently acknowledged the incident, describing its decision to exploit employees' expectations as inappropriate. “Using the rings as a lure to gain employees’ attention was an unfortunate mistake,” it said in an official statement. The organization explained that its security concerns stemmed from an earlier cyberattack in which employee credentials were compromised through a similar fraudulent communication. Hackers had reportedly used those credentials to access company systems and subsequently extort the organization, prompting additional efforts to improve employee awareness. The company also disclosed plans to distribute more than 275 commemorative items among players, coaches, employees and other individuals associated with the franchise. According to the organization, those gifts, comprising championship rings and other jewellery, carry a combined estimated value exceeding $3.7 million. However, the distribution arrangements have attracted attention because several assistant coaches initially received empty presentation boxes during the championship celebration. The assistants are expected to obtain their rings later, although numerous long-time arena employees and business personnel reportedly remain excluded entirely. The organization has not specified exactly how many workers will receive individual rings rather than alternative jewellery under its announced distribution arrangements. Via Arstechnica
articles.author: Efosa Udinmwen

A new NYT Connections puzzle appears at midnight each day for your time zone – which means that some people are always playing 'today's game' while others are playing 'yesterday's'. If you're looking for Wednesday's puzzle instead then click here: NYT Connections hints and answers for Wednesday, October 28 (game #1235) . Good morning! Let's play Connections, the NYT's clever word game that challenges you to group answers in various categories. It can be tough, so read on if you need Connections hints. What should you do once you've finished? Why, play some more word games of course. I've also got daily Strands hints and answers and Quordle hints and answers articles if you need help for those too, while Marc's Wordle today page covers the original viral word game. SPOILER WARNING: Information about NYT Connections today is below, so don't read on if you don't want to know the answers. NYT Connections today (game #1236) - today's words (Image credit: New York Times) Today's NYT Connections words are… TUXEDO TRAFFIC LIGHT ROMAN EMPEROR PARKING METER CANDY CORN NEAPOLITAN PIGGY BANK TYPEWRITER WISHING WELL GOTHIC ANTARCTICA CALICO WADDLE SANS PAYPHONE NYT Connections today (game #1236) - hint #1 - group hints What are some clues for today's NYT Connections groups? YELLOW: Insert cash in these GREEN: All linked to a non-flying bird BLUE: Type with missing words PURPLE: Triple shade Need more clues? We're firmly in spoiler territory now, but read on if you want to know what the four theme answers are for today's NYT Connections puzzles… NYT Connections today (game #1236) - hint #2 - group answers What are the answers for today's NYT Connections groups? YELLOW: THINGS YOU PUT COINS INTO GREEN: ASSOCIATED WITH PENGUINS BLUE: ENDS OF FAMOUS FONTS PURPLE: THINGS THAT FEATURE THREE COLORS Right, the answers are below, so DO NOT SCROLL ANY FURTHER IF YOU DON'T WANT TO SEE THEM. NYT Connections today (game #1236) - the answers (Image credit: New York Times) The answers to today's Connections, game #1236, are… YELLOW: THINGS YOU PUT COINS INTO: PARKING METER, PAYPHONE, PIGGY BANK, WISHING WELL GREEN: ASSOCIATED WITH PENGUINS: ANTARCTICA, EMPEROR, TUXEDO, WADDLE BLUE: ENDS OF FAMOUS FONTS: GOTHIC, ROMAN, SANS, TYPEWRITER PURPLE: THINGS THAT FEATURE THREE COLORS: CALICO, CANDY CORN, NEAPOLITAN, TRAFFIC LIGHT My rating: Hard My score: 1 mistake When I was a full-time journalist, I was a peak procrastinator and would often spend ages choosing the exact font for an article instead of just sticking with one (I think it may be apparent here why I am a former full-time journalist). I came to peace with it in the end and considered it part of the thinking process — but it also meant that the tiles SANS, ROMAN, TYPEWRITER and GOTHIC immediately jumped out at me. Not that I’d ever write anything using Comic Sans of course (people have been sentenced to prison for less). From here I thought I spotted four types of penguins and included CALICO instead of WADDLE because I had some vague memory of Calico penguins when I should have been thinking of Calico cats. Anyway, no harm done as I got them with the next go and escaped with just one mistake. Yesterday's NYT Connections answers (Wednesday, October 28, 2026, game #1235) YELLOW: ROMANTIC LIKING: ATTRACTION, CRUSH, FEELINGS, INTEREST GREEN: COMPONENTS OF AN EMAIL: ATTACHMENT, BODY, SIGNATURE, SUBJECT BLUE: NASA MARS ROVERS: CURIOSITY, OPPORTUNITY, PERSEVERANCE, SPIRIT PURPLE: HOMOPHONES OF PATHS: COARSE, RODE, ROUT, WEIGH What is NYT Connections? NYT Connections is one of several increasingly popular word games made by the New York Times. It challenges you to find groups of four items that share something in common, and each group has a different difficulty level: green is easy, yellow a little harder, blue often quite tough and purple usually very difficult. On the plus side, you don't technically need to solve the final one, as you'll be able to answer that one by a…

articles.title: SteelSeries Sensei Pro Mini review: small in size, big in performance
articles.content: SteelSeries Sensei Pro Mini: Review The Sensei Pro Mini brings pro-grade wireless performance to those who prefer less of a handful, thanks to its state-of-the-art polling technology and ceaseless power. It has the same symmetrical shape as its larger sibling but on a smaller scale. Its size should prove suitable for those with smaller hands, allowing them to get a secure grip around the entire unit. At just 49g, it’s very light, too — lighter than the standard model by 4g — which makes it easy to maneuver. The sidewalls have a pronounced cinch that forces you to clamp your thumb and ring finger further inwards than is typical, which some may prefer for added security. Grip tape is included in the box if you require more traction, which is entirely possible given the smoothness of the outer shell. The central hump might prove contentious in terms of fit, though: in my experience, it didn’t sit back far enough in my hand, landing underneath my knuckles rather than in the middle of my palm. (Image credit: Future) To customize and tweak the Sensei Pro Mini, you can use SteelSeries’ GG peripheral software. Here you can rebind all six buttons, with a fair amount of mapping options available, including keyboard inputs and shortcuts for media controls and system actions. You’ll find some standard performance tweaks as well, including DPI adjustments, although the range is larger than you’ll usually find on other gaming mice (between 1 to 65,000). There are five presets to customize, which you can cycle through using the DPI button underneath the mouse. There are more advanced tweaks in addition to these, though. You can adjust the click response between 0ms and 20ms, and set the lift-off and landing distances independently, each with a range of 0.7 to 1.7 (presumably this refers to millimeters, though no unit of measurement is given). You can also enable a feature called Scroll Jump Protection, which ignores your first scroll unless a second is performed within a certain time of the first. This threshold is adjustable between 100ms and 1500ms. Motion Sync and Angle Snapping toggles are here as well, with the latter featuring a slider with 10 levels to adjust its straightening effect. (Image credit: Future) This isn’t all, though: a further section lets you adjust acceleration, with several graph curve presets available to alter cursor speed relative to movement speed, as well as the angle of the mouse’s sensor by 45 degrees either side of center to match the natural angle of your hand movements. Then there are the polling and sensor adjustments. You can set the ultra-wideband (UWB) polling rate and the sensor report rate independently, each with a range of 125Hz to 8KHz (with added 9KHz overpolling). There are five presets containing various combinations of both rates, which can be cycled through using the button on the UWB base station. GG is clearly laid out and proved fast and stable during my time with it. It also contains explanations for many of its settings, which is something I’m always glad to see. One minor gripe I had is that the actual area to make adjustments and customizations opens in a second window, which is somewhat inconvenient. (Image credit: Future) The first thing that’s noticeable about the Sensei Pro Mini’s performance is just how smoothly it glides. This is no doubt thanks to the large PTFE skates underneath. There’s almost no friction when gliding over a mouse mat, which makes the Sensei Pro Mini feel incredibly gratifying to fling around, yet also allows for super-controlled slow movements. Next is the Sensei Pro Mini’s buttons. Clicks are light and snappy enough for quick spams, yet still provide enough feedback to allow for controlled inputs. They also have just enough dampening to make them satisfying to use. The side buttons are great to use as well, being easy to reach and offering a clicky, tactile feel. The same is true of the middle click, and I didn’t trigger miscrolls when using it, since the…

articles.titleFa: بررسی SteelSeries Sensei Pro Mini: کوچک در اندازه، بزرگ در عملکرد
articles.summaryFa: ماوس بی‌سیم SteelSeries Sensei Pro Mini با فناوری پیشرفته، عملکرد حرفه‌ای و طراحی ارگونومیک برای کاربران با دستان کوچک را ارائه می‌دهد. این ماوس تنها ۴۹ گرم وزن دارد و قابلیت‌های سفارشی‌سازی بالایی را از طریق نرم‌افزار GG SteelSeries به ارمغان می‌آورد، از جمله تنظیم DPI تا ۶۵۰۰۰. مزیت‌های دیگر شامل ویژگی‌هایی مثل پاسخ‌گویی کلیک و تنظیمات فاصله برداشتن و نشستن نیز وجود دارد.
articles.summaryEn: The SteelSeries Sensei Pro Mini is a lightweight wireless mouse designed for users with smaller hands, featuring advanced performance capabilities and a symmetrical shape. Weighing in at just 49g, it offers extensive customization options through SteelSeries' GG software, including adjustable DPI levels up to 65,000 and various performance tweaks. Other notable features include click response adjustments and lift-off distance settings.

articles.title: Bigger than Bing or Xbox: Microsoft’s OpenAI haul reaches $10B in quarterly revenue
articles.content: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella at OpenAI’s DevDay in November 2023. (GeekWire File Photo / Todd Bishop) OpenAI generated $10 billion in revenue for Microsoft in the quarter ended Sept. 30, about 11% of the Redmond company’s total revenue, according to its quarterly filing Wednesday . The amount is up sharply. In the fiscal year that ended in June, Microsoft recorded $24.1 billion in revenue from its business with OpenAI, or about $6 billion a quarter on average. That $10 billion surpasses some of Microsoft’s longest-running businesses. Xbox brought in $5.4 billion in the quarter. Search and advertising, which includes its Bing search engine, generated $6.6 billion. Windows licenses sold through PC makers, along with Surface and other Microsoft devices, brought in $3.6 billion. Related Microsoft Azure revenue surges 48% to $33.2B, beating expectations as cloud and AI demand grows The total covers revenue-sharing payments from OpenAI, as well as other business between the companies, such as OpenAI’s use of Azure to train and run its AI models. Microsoft didn’t say how much came from each, or how much of Azure’s growth came from OpenAI. Azure revenue rose 48% to $33.2 billion in the quarter, beating Wall Street’s expectations and the company’s own forecast of 44% to 45% growth. Microsoft has begun disclosing its revenue from OpenAI because its stake of about 24% makes OpenAI a “related party” under accounting rules, requiring it to report the business they do with each other. Microsoft first reported the number in its annual report in July, as a full-year total. This is the first time it has given a quarterly figure. The original AI alliance: Microsoft first invested in OpenAI in 2019, eventually committing $13 billion , and became its exclusive cloud provider. ChatGPT ran on Azure when it launched in late 2022. The companies have loosened their ties since then. OpenAI restructured as a public benefit corporation in October 2025 , and Microsoft gave up its right of first refusal to supply OpenAI’s computing capacity. OpenAI committed to buy an additional $250 billion in Azure services. An April 2026 agreement gave OpenAI broader freedom to use other cloud providers. OpenAI has also agreed to keep sharing revenue with Microsoft through 2030. In addition, Microsoft sells access to OpenAI’s models to business customers through its Azure OpenAI Service, and the models became the foundation for its Copilot products, putting Microsoft at the front of the generative AI boom. That revenue comes from Microsoft’s own customers, so it isn’t part of the $10 billion. Microsoft, for its part, now builds its own AI models and offers models from Anthropic and others. Many customers, not a few: Asked by Bernstein Research analyst Mark Moerdler whether AI growth on Azure was coming from big businesses or AI-native companies, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella didn’t mention OpenAI. He said he doesn’t want Azure’s AI business to depend on a few big customers, and that broad adoption by businesses is just getting started. Nadella described it as “a decade-long thing,” and contrasted it with relying on “four customers who buy a lot of capacity from you” to show a few quarters of growth. That, he said, is “not a business as far as I’m concerned.” He added that Microsoft has large customers who want to buy capacity, “and as long as the pricing is right, we may sell them some. If not, we will be patient.” Later in the call, Goldman Sachs analyst Gabriela Borges brought up the fact that OpenAI made up 11% of revenue. Nadella didn’t address the number but praised OpenAI’s latest models and said customers are increasingly mixing models from different companies, or training their own. He cited Microsoft’s tools for routing each task to whichever AI model handles it best. If you use AI coding agents, Nadella said, you want Anthropic and…

articles.title: I put three sub-AU$1,300 stick vacuums with auto-empty docks to the test — here's which one is actually worth your money
articles.content: Shopping for a premium appliance — like a new cordless vacuum and accompanying auto-empty dock — is no easy task. Before taking the plunge, you need to consider a couple of factors, including your budget, how large (or small) your home is and storage for your new purchase. Bonus points if you have kids or pets and their messes to consider, too. Thankfully, Black Friday 2026 is just around the corner, and it's the perfect time to upgrade or save on a new cordless vacuum and auto-empty station. As a home appliance reviewer, it's my job to assess new products and make recommendations based on my findings — especially in the lead-up to a major deals fest like Cyber Weekend. Over the past three months, I tested three premium cordless vacuum cleaners from major floorcare brands in Australia: Dyson, Shark and Tineco. Dyson and Shark don't need much of an introduction, as leaders (and competitors) in the space. Tineco, on the other hand, has long held its own in the wet-to-dry vacuum realm, and has recently expanded its cordless vacuum lineup. I compared pricing, suction power, docking stations and battery life to inform my final recommendation for those looking for the perfect vacuum pairing this Black Friday. So let's cut to the chase — here's how the Dyson V10 Konical + Auto-Empty Dok , Shark PowerDetect Speed Clean & Empty and Tineco Pure One Station A70S Pet compare. Shark Home PowerDetect Speed Clean & Empty Shark's PowerDetect Speed Clean & Empty vacuum cleaner and dock deliver enhanced suction power, multidirectional cleaning and a tangle-free brush head. Dyson V10 Konical Vacuum Cleaner + Auto-Empty Dok Dyson's V10 Konical vacuum cleaner and Auto-Empty Dok delivers fade-free suction power, can detangle long hairs and fur, and features a new self-cleaning dock for the brand. Tineco Australia Pure One Station A70s Pet Tineco's latest 3-in-1 cordless vacuum and self-cleaning dock is designed for homes with kids and pets, featuring 200 AW suction power, a ClogLess cleaner head, and an advanced filtration system. Price and specifications Dyson Shark Tom's Guide / Lucy Scotting At full price, all three vacuums sit comfortably in the premium category. The most expensive is Tineco's Pure One A70S, priced at AU$1,299. Snug in the middle is Dyson's V10 Konical at AU$999, which leaves the most affordable title to Shark's PowerDetect Speed at AU$799. All three vacuums come with replaceable battery packs and similar attachments — i.e. a crevice tool, a mini upholstery head and an anti-tangle main brush head with LED lights — but there are a few exceptions. The Dyson V10 Konical comes with the brand's signature conical-shaped detangling cleaner head, which is fantastic for sucking up hair and fur more easily. Tineco's A70S has a ClogLess feature on the main cleaning head, which switches the suction port to a larger size based on the debris you're sucking up. Shark's device has reverse cleaning, so it will suck up dust no matter which direction you swipe, and it also comes with a fragrance puck to pop in the dock to keep odour away. Dyson, Shark and Tineco cordless vacuum specs Dyson V10 Konical & Auto-Empty Dok Shark PowerDetect Speed Clean & Empty Tineco Pure One Station A70S Pet Price AU$999 AU$799 AU$1,299 Weight 1.63kg 3.2kg 4kg Warranty Not specified Not specified 2 years Dimensions (vacuum unit) 113cm × 7.87cm × 20cm 26cm W × 35.5cm D × 114.5cm H Not available Dimensions (when stationed) 118cm × 6.69cm × 17cm 117.5cm H × 26cm W × 45.5cm D Not available Bin size (dock) 2.5L 2L 2.5L Maximum runtime 60 minutes 60 minutes 80 minutes Suction power 150AW 350AW 200AW Suction Power Tom's Guide / Lucy Scotting Dyson When it comes to measuring suction power, most vacuum brands consider either air watts (AW) or revolutions per minute (RPM). The key difference is that air watts measure how much real suction and cleaning power a vacuum cleaner produces, rather than how fast the motor rotates. articles.title: One step closer to the Terminator? Experts reveal robot with 'real muscles' strong enough to jump, swim and grasp
articles.content: Laboratory-grown muscle tissue has been developed to improve robot dexterity and motion Researchers working at ETH Zurich have demonstrated tissue-based muscle actuators that flex The actuators enable small robots to jump and swim, as well as walk and grasp Flesh-covered robots that can walk, jump, swim and move among us may be closer than we think. Researchers working out of ETH Zurich have been busy developing muscle actuators from centimeter-scale living tissue. These muscle actuators are the latest in a design program, and motion has been improved over 10 times compared with previous iterations. In designing the biohybrid robots, the researchers have found that it isn’t all about the volume of muscle tissue. How the muscle and the bone (or in this case, an “artificial scaffold”) interact is also important. Grown from mouse muscle cells, the results are being viewed as a new way of building robots. Biohybrid muscle The project is run from the ETH Zurich Soft Robotics Lab and is overseen by Professor Robert Katzschmann, who states that “We’re just beginning to build robots in a more natural way.” The research focuses on biohybrids, which basically refers to integrating biological materials like muscle tissue with artificial, man-made materials like electronics or mechanical scaffold. Design of the robots has evolved through the research to the current state, where the muscle tissue is secured to the scaffold using grooves that the tissue can attach to. Meanwhile, the robots are currently limited to motion within a nutrient solution intended to feed the muscles and keep them “alive.” An interesting result from the research is that not all muscle actuators behave in the same way. This “natural variability” that comes from using living tissue contrasts with what is achievable with manufactured components. Flesh for cyborgs Development of flesh muscles for robots has taken place over several years, with designs built on computer. Over what has been called an “iterative process” by co-lead author of the published study Aiste Balciunaite, the idea of “a fixed form for our muscle geometry” was eschewed in favor of designing “the whole thing from scratch on the computer.” “With previous systems, you sometimes had to look under a microscope to see the flexing,” Balciunaite adds, highlighting how far the project has come. The video above demonstrates the range of movement that can be performed by the muscle actuators, with the activity now visible to the naked eye. Measuring over 1cm, the bioactuators can move and grasp, and are shown here swimming. Other biohybrid robots have been programmed to walk, managing to cover 6.2 millimeters a second. Will these bio-attached structures develop into an army of time traveling, human-destroying cyborgs? Probably not, and as they have applications for exploration and medicine, we shouldn't be too concerned.

articles.title: ULA's Vulcan rocket is set to return to flight on Friday the 13th
articles.content: United Launch Alliance announced Wednesday it plans to return its Vulcan rocket to service on November 13, nine months after a solid rocket booster anomaly threw the company's 2026 launch schedule into oblivion. The return-to-flight mission will launch 40 satellites for the Amazon Leo broadband constellation, the first of 38 Vulcan flights Amazon has booked to deploy the bulk of its network. The mission will lift off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida, and ULA said the launch date is pending range approval. The launch is critical for ULA after its new flagship rocket suffered nozzle failures on its solid rocket boosters on two of its first four missions, most recently during a flight in February. In both cases, the rocket overcame the nozzle failure and completed its mission, but officials at the US Space Force, ULA's primary customer, lost confidence in Vulcan. Read full article Comments

articles.title: Here's Everything Apple Announced This Week
articles.content: It's been a busy October for Apple, and just this week, we got a new OLED iPad mini , an ‌OLED‌ MacBook Pro with a touch display, a new M6 ‌MacBook Pro‌, and an M6 iMac . Subscribe to the MacRumors YouTube channel for more videos. If you missed the news over the last three days, we've rounded up all our coverage in one spot, so it's easy to take a look back. The ‌MacBook Pro‌ got the biggest update, and it's now the first Mac with an ‌OLED‌ display and touch support. It's a little bit thinner and lighter than the mini-LED models, which are also still on sale, but it unfortunately uses the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips Apple introduced earlier this year. It also got a Dynamic Island , a glowing Apple logo, and a new speaker setup, but prices went up too. The ‌OLED‌ models have a $400 premium over comparable mini-LED models. Apple's other big update was the ‌iPad mini‌, which also has an ‌OLED‌ display. It's the second iPad to get ‌OLED‌ after the iPad Pro , and it's the first ‌iPad‌ with an official water and dust resistance rating. It uses a new acoustic display setup, helping it earn an IP67 rating, so it'll hold up to brief submersion and splashing. The base 14-inch ‌MacBook Pro‌ and the ‌iMac‌ got M6 chips, but not much else. articles.title: As US ties fray, Europe plans first undersea cable link to Greenland
articles.content: The European Union plans to create the first subsea Internet cable directly connecting Europe to Greenland. The Pan-Arctic Cable project could also extend to Canada and eventually link with Japan and South Korea, notably bypassing the United States. The Pan-Arctic Cable is described as a European Union flagship project in a European Commission joint communication published on October 20, 2026. The policy document describes a new European strategy for the Arctic that supports “a sovereign, secure and resilient submarine cable connection linking Greenland directly to the EU,” while also suggesting that “like-minded partners like Canada” could provide a stepping stone for future cable expansion toward Asia. “It is interesting that this project is even being considered, because five years ago it would have seemed like not a particularly commercially attractive proposition,” Elisabeth Braw , a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council who leads the Threats to the Global Maritime Order Initiative, told Ars. “But the fact that it's being considered is very much on trend and a sign of our times.” Read full article Comments

articles.content: Surprise! The new 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro models with OLED displays have a glowing Apple logo , a beloved feature that was phased out a decade ago. In a hands-on video shared on his YouTube channel UrAvgConsumer, Judner Aura showed off the glowing Apple logo and revealed that its brightness is tied to the MacBook Pro's display brightness. If you turn up the display brightness, the logo gets brighter, and vice versa. The glowing logo worked the same way on older MacBooks. Skip ahead to the one-minute mark of the video to see the glowing Apple logo. Apple never publicly commented on why it removed the glowing logo, but many customers have long wanted it back, and the company has evidently listened. The new MacBook Pro models are available to pre-order now and launch Friday, November 6. articles.title: Peptide peddlers cheer as RFK Jr. unilaterally grants access, overruling FDA
articles.content: Anti-vaccine Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy has unilaterally passed a rule that will allow specialty pharmacies to sell six specific peptide drugs, overruling scientists at the Food and Drug Administration. The peptides are popular among members of Kennedy's Make America Health Again movement and many prominent MAHA figures and Kennedy allies sell them. Kennedy said he uses some of the peptides and called himself a "big fan." But FDA scientists continue to say there is insufficient evidence to show if they're effective and they are potentially dangerous. In 2023, the safety concerns led the FDA to remove the six peptides from a list of drugs that can be made by specialty pharmacies called compounding pharmacies—which make customized formulations of drugs for patients, or, in cases such as this, specialty drugs in bulk. Kennedy's new rule sidesteps the need to formally undo that FDA action. The rule is titled "Enforcement Discretion Policy Regarding 503A Compounding Using Certain Peptide Bulk Drug Substances" and was made available Wednesday on the Federal Register , with the final publication data set for October 30. The rule does not change the regulatory status of the peptide; instead, it states the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) will no longer take enforcement action against compounding pharmacies for making the peptides, essentially giving them a green light to freely produce and sell them. Kennedy had quietly proposed this rule earlier this month. Read full article Comments
articles.author: Beth Mole

articles.title: How Accurate Were Rumors About Apple's OLED Touchscreen MacBook Pro?
articles.content: Rumors about Apple's work on a touchscreen OLED MacBook Pro started in 2023, when Bloomberg 's Mark Gurman said there would be a MacBook Pro with an ‌OLED‌ display and a touchscreen, but ‌OLED‌ rumors date back even further. We heard a lot about the new Mac over the last few years, and we thought we'd take a look back to see what was right and what was wrong. OLED 2016 - In 2016, ETNews said Apple was considering ‌OLED‌ displays for future MacBooks. 2019 - The Elec said Apple was in talks with Samsung about ‌OLED‌ displays for a future 16-inch ‌MacBook Pro‌. 2021 - The Elec said a future MacBook would use an ‌OLED‌ display with a two-stack tandem structure , which is what Apple announced today. 2023 - ETNews claimed Apple was sourcing OLED panels in 14-inch and 16-inch sizes for the ‌MacBook Pro‌, which turned out to be accurate. 2023 - Apple analyst Ming-Chi Kuo said Apple would release the first MacBook with an OLED display by the end of 2024 at the earliest, which was incorrect. Touch 2023 - Bloomberg 's ‌Mark Gurman‌ was the first to report on a touch display. In January 2023, he said Apple was working on an ‌OLED‌ ‌MacBook Pro‌ with a touchscreen. 2025 - Kuo said in September 2025 that the ‌OLED‌ ‌MacBook Pro‌ would have touch sensors integrated into the display panel's top layer, which was correct. No Notch/Dynamic Island 2024 - Omdia said in December 2024 that Apple would remove the notch from the ‌MacBook Pro‌ "in a few years," replacing it with a hole-punch camera. The hole-punch aspect wasn't quite correct. 2025 - In August 2025, Omdia said an ‌OLED‌ MacBook coming in 2026 would have an iPhone-like Dynamic Island cutout instead of a notch . 2025 - In October 2025, Gurman said the ‌OLED‌ ‌MacBook Pro‌ would have a "so-called hole-punch design" with a "display area around the sensor" similar to the ‌Dynamic Island‌. 2026 - In February 2026, Gurman described the ‌Dynamic Island‌ as interactive and able to contextually expand based on the app or Mac feature in use. Hinge 2025 - Gurman was the first to mention a reinforced hinge that would keep the display from moving when touched. Design 2024 - In November 2024, Gurman said the ‌MacBook Pro‌ would have a thinner design , which was accurate. 2026 - In October 2026, Gurman said he didn't expect the ‌MacBook Pro‌ would be "significantly thinner," tempering expectations. 2026 - In October 2026, he said the ‌MacBook Pro‌ models would be "significantly lighter." Chips 2025 - In October 2025, Gurman predicted the ‌OLED‌ ‌MacBook Pro‌ models would use M6-series chips, and in November , he specified M6 Pro and M6 Max chips. 2026 - In June 2026, Gurman said there would be no M6 Pro or M6 Max chips , and the ‌OLED‌ ‌MacBook Pro‌ would instead use M5 Pro and M5 Max chips. 2026 - In September 2026, Omdia said the ‌OLED‌ ‌MacBook Pro‌ would have an M5 Ultra chip option , which was wrong. Pricing 2026 - In March 2026, Gurman said the ‌OLED‌ ‌MacBook Pro‌ models would be more expensive and would be above the mini-LED ‌MacBook Pro‌ models, which was correct. 2026 - Just a day before the ‌MacBook Pro‌ models were announced, Gurman accurately predicted the $2,899 and $3,399 pricing. Naming March 2026 - Gurman suggested Apple was working on a " MacBook Ultra ," but he did hedge and say Apple might not use the Ultra naming. April 2026 - Macworld claimed Apple would release a ‌MacBook Ultra‌ in late 2026 or early 2027. October 2026 - MacRumors ' Joe Rossignol speculated that Apple could call the new MacBook the "MacBook Studio," but that didn't happen. articles.title: Price hikes can’t stop YouTube Premium from hitting new subscriber records
articles.content: TL;DR Alphabet published its Q3 2026 financial report this afternoon. In sharing the news, CEO Sundar Pichai announced that YouTube Music and Premium now have over 150M subscribers. That figure includes trial subscriptions, but it’s also up from the 125M the company shared earlier this year. Google — sorry, Alphabet — is sharing its latest financial report today, detailing the company’s Q3 2026 performance. And as you should only expect, that’s full of tons of data points about AI, token usage, and all things Search. But it also offer us an all-too-rare peek into how things are doing for one of the biggest streaming services around, as Google shares new YouTube subscriber figures. As CEO Sundar Pichai explains , YouTube Music and YouTube Premium now count over 150 million subscribers around the world. This past spring, that figure was only at 125 million .

articles.title: Sonos Beam Ultra review: The compact Dolby Atmos powerhouse we’ve been waiting for
articles.content: Sonos Beam Ultra: Cheat sheet Price: 3.5/5 Sound quality: 4.5/5 Design: 5/5 Features: 5/5 Overall score: 4.5 Best for: Dolby Atmos in mid-size spaces I’ve spent years championing the original Sonos Beam and Beam Gen 2 as the best soundbars for anyone living in the “real world,” a.k.a. living arrangements where cavernous ceilings and elaborate home theaters aren’t the norm. But as much as I loved the Beam Gen 2, the lack of physical height channels was noticeable despite impressive software-simulated Dolby Atmos for a soundbar of its size. The newer Sonos Beam Ultra ($699) addresses that shortcoming with 7.2.1 Atmos powered by dedicated upward-firing drivers and a completely redesigned acoustic system. It also arrives alongside Sonos 27, the company's next-generation OS, which introduces smarter controls, AI-powered features and new ways to connect speakers throughout the home. And somehow, Sonos has squeezed all of that audio hardware into a soundbar barely wider than its predecessor. On paper, it's the upgrade I've been waiting for. But what surprised me most, as you’ll read in this Sonos Beam Ultra review, was just how much bigger it sounds. Sonos Beam Ultra: Specs Price $699 / £699 Weight 6.35 lbs Speakers 9 drivers (5 tweeters, 4 woofers) Ports HDMI eARC, USB-C (line-in/Ethernet via adapter) Audio formats Dolby Atmos Colors Black, White Voice assistants Sonos Voice Control, Amazon Alexa Connectivity Wi-Fi 6, Bluetooth 5.3, Apple AirPlay 2, Spotify Connect Sonos Beam Ultra review: What I like Genuine upward-firing Dolby Atmos delivers a dramatic upgrade over the Beam Gen 2. Exceptionally clear dialogue, sleek design and effortless room calibration make it ideal for smaller spaces. Sonos 27 and flexible wireless surrounds make an already impressive soundbar even more versatile. The Beam Ultra brings some meaningful improvements over its predecessor, but it's the combination of immersive sound, effortless setup and Sonos' increasingly versatile ecosystem that makes it such a compelling upgrade. Sound quality: Genuine height, wider dispersion and crystal-clear dialogue (Image credit: Tom's Guide) The acoustic jump between the Sonos Beam Ultra vs. Sonos Beam (Gen 2) is night and day. Where the Beam Gen 2 relied on a single center tweeter, four mid-woofers and three passive radiators, the Beam Ultra packs nine Class-D amplifiers powering five tweeters (including two angled upward into directional horns) and four woofers. Cueing up the low-altitude trench run in Top Gun: Maverick showed off the new architecture immediately. Where jet passes used to feel broad but horizontally constrained, they now climb the bedroom walls and sweep across the ceiling. It’s an authentic three-dimensional sound field rather than an algorithmic trick. Dialogue clarity is equally top-tier. Sonos introduced an AI-assisted Speech Enhancement algorithm here that rivals Sony’s best dialogue processing. Even against dense orchestral scores or combat sound effects, spoken lines remain isolated, centered and effortless to understand without skewing unnatural or sharp. Design and setup: Home-friendly aesthetics and painless installation (Image credit: Tom's Guide) I installed the Beam Ultra beneath a wall-mounted Samsung Frame TV in my bedroom, and visually, it looks exceptional. The matte finish and uniform micro-perforated grille adhere faithfully to Sonos's minimalist ethos. At just 2.5 inches tall, it keeps a slender profile that sits well below screen bezels, while its slightly wider footprint makes it look right at home anchored beneath 55- and 65-inch sets. The physical setup was ridiculously simple. Because the Frame routes through a One Connect box, swapping out my Beam Gen 2 literally required plugging in two cords: the power cable and the included HDMI eARC lead. From there, the Sonos app recognized the bar had been powered on automatically. More importantly, Sonos finally added a fast Trueplay routine. Instead of pacing around the room waving…

articles.title: Scaling Agentic AI Coding Assistants in a Regulated Enterprise
articles.content: Key Takeaways Published evidence on AI coding productivity is genuinely mixed — from a 55.8% speed-up on a greenfield task to a 19% slowdown for experienced developers in mature codebases — so an enterprise rollout must measure its own outcomes rather than assume a gain. Agentic tools differ from autocomplete because they act: they read files, run commands, and call external systems, which makes permissions, not prompts, the primary control surface. Central to our model are centrally managed deny rules, deterministic hooks for policy that must always apply, reviewed skills for repeatable workflows, and an allowlist of approved tool integrations. AI-generated code has to go through the exact same review, testing, and security processes as human-written code; we see that developers who use assistants tend to produce less secure code, which they are also more confident in. Scale enablement for hundreds of engineers is a platform issue -- curate workflows, share guardrails, and improve the feedback loop, not a series of tool demos. Executive Summary Agentic coding assistants can change files, execute shell commands, and use tools for engineers. That makes them useful for removing tedious work from engineering processes, but it also creates serious adoption challenges inside a regulated enterprise. Based on experience leading agentic AI automation programs and supporting more than 600 engineers at a large financial-services organization, this article describes an enablement architecture built on four layers: governance, guardrails, curated knowledge, and integration. It connects each layer to specific configuration choices, explains why existing software delivery controls must remain the final checkpoint, examines how to assess results when research points in different directions, and acknowledges where the approach falls short. Introduction Adoption of AI assistance is now the norm rather than the exception. DORA's 2025 research reports that about 90% of surveyed technology professionals use AI, while 30% have little or no trust in the code it produces [11]. The 2025 Stack Overflow survey found 84% of developers using or planning to use AI tools, but only 14.1% using AI agents daily [22]. That gap — broad use of assistants, cautious use of agents — is where most enterprises sit. Moving from suggestion to action changes the risk profile. An autocomplete suggestion is inert until a human accepts it; an agent can run a migration script, push a branch, or call an internal API. In a bank, that difference matters to security, audit, and model-risk teams. Engineers have at their disposal a powerful tool with default settings; also, each team develops its own prompts, and governance comes in late to impose restrictions, which in turn erode trust. As an alternative, we see here that what is put forth is to treat agentic AI as an internal platform with its own architecture. Background An agent, in the sense used by Anthropic's engineering guidance, is a system in which the model directs its own process and tool use, as opposed to a workflow that follows a fixed code path; that guidance also recommends starting with the simplest solution that works [7]. Coding agents connect to external systems through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open JSON-RPC-based protocol in which servers expose tools, resources, and prompts. The specification is explicit that tools represent arbitrary code execution and that hosts should obtain user consent before invoking them, while noting the protocol cannot enforce this on its own [6]. Engineers in this environment use several assistants, including GitHub Copilot, Windsurf, Codex, and Claude Code. The examples below use Claude Code's configuration model because it documents the relevant controls clearly [1]–[5]; the architecture depends on the control types, not the product: Control type Question it answers Typical mechanism Central policy What is never allowed? articles.title: I Built an AI Model That Outperformed AWS and Google on Image Moderation
articles.content: I started working on Blue-Eye because I was curious about something: how difficult would it actually be to build an image moderation model that could compete with the commercial APIs everyone uses? If you're building anything that allows user-uploaded images, content moderation eventually becomes a problem you have to deal with. The straightforward approach is to integrate something like AWS Rekognition or Google Cloud Vision. They handle the infrastructure, you send an image, and you get a moderation result back. It's convenient, but you're also paying for requests and relying on someone else's model, with limited control over how it makes decisions. There are open models available too, of course, but I wanted to see how far I could push one myself. Not by training some enormous vision model from scratch, but by taking a strong pretrained model, fine-tuning it for a specific task, and seeing how it compared with existing services. The catch was that I didn't have a research lab, a team, or a large compute budget. I was working independently, using free and community-supported resources wherever I could. Training a model on millions of images under those constraints sounded a little ambitious, but I figured it was worth trying. That experiment turned into Blue-Eye , a 303-million-parameter image classifier built on Meta's DINOv3 architecture. It predicts whether an image is safe, suggestive, or explicit, and it was fine-tuned on approximately 2.6 million images covering both real photographs and anime or illustrated content. When I eventually ran my main benchmark, Blue-Eye reached 88.9% accuracy on 3,000 real photographs , compared with 87.3% for AWS Rekognition and 83.5% for Google Cloud Vision SafeSearch. That's the comparison shown in the chart above. I wouldn't call that proof of being universally better than those services, especially since the evaluation uses my own dataset and category mappings. But seeing an independently developed model perform that competitively was encouraging, and I wanted to share how I got there. The problem with classifying something as NSFW. One thing that makes NSFW detection tricky is that simply detecting nudity or exposed skin isn't enough. Think about how many perfectly ordinary images contain a lot of visible skin. Beach photographs, fitness content, medical images, breastfeeding, and certain kinds of artwork are obvious examples. A classifier that gets too aggressive can end up flagging harmless images, which isn't particularly useful if you're trying to build a reliable moderation system. Then there's the more ambiguous content. An image might be sexualized without being explicit, and the boundary isn't always something even two people would agree on. Different platforms also have different ideas of what should be allowed. For Blue-Eye, I went with three classes rather than a simple safe-or-unsafe prediction. Safe covers non-sexual content, including things like swimwear and medical images. Suggestive covers sexualized but non-explicit content, while explicit covers explicit nudity and sexual activity. The model produces three softmax scores and selects the highest-scoring class as its prediction. Developers can also use those scores to choose their own thresholds, although they shouldn't be treated as perfectly calibrated confidence estimates without additional testing. I liked this approach because it gives platforms some flexibility instead of forcing everyone to use exactly the same moderation policy. Of course, getting a model to consistently distinguish those classes is easier said than done. The suggestive category in particular turned out to be one of the more difficult parts of the task. Training a 303M-parameter model on 2.6 million images. For the backbone, I chose DINOv3 ViT-L/16 , Meta's pretrained vision transformer. articles.title: Modernizing Cloud Admission Control: Off the Global Read Path
articles.content: Key Takeaways Admission control sits on the critical path of every resource creation, so any synchronous global dependency on its read path quietly becomes a fleet-wide failure domain. One should distinguish between policy choices that can evolve gradually and those that quickly alter consumer statistics. An impeccable system should compute overcommitment indices, predict demand, and refresh data on all resources that supply dependable data about their current capability. Using an outdated read can be beneficial only when proper boundaries are in place: a soft limit provides an incentive to read responsibly, but a hard limit ensures safe failure only after due notice. The world reading dependence is severed, and the dangers move to snapshot transfer, which should occur cell by cell, in the same way as code deployment happens. A strangler-fig decomposition with shadow decisions and decision-diff metrics is a low-risk way to replace a monolithic admission service without changing capacity outcomes during migration. Executive Summary The limitations of Cloud admission control pertain to three factors before running a virtual machine or disk. The admission control process is important and must take place in real time, which is why the convoluted state of the system’s global resources is problematic. This paper describes a new admission control process that divides it and assigns an old state of resources to the isolated resource change. This fosters autonomous functioning of each entity since they do not need to be aware about what is going on in the system in total. The paper covers fail-stable patterns of admission control, analysis of latency, specimen system state management, and a gradual migration from the current architecture to a new one being built in its place. Introduction Autoscalers do not scale out, deploys tie up and which in turn blocks recovery when we need it most. Admission control is a behind-the-scenes player until it breaks. Borg made admission control, together with overcommitment, a first-class part of achieving high utilization [1]. Kubernetes exposes the same idea through admission webhooks and quality-of-service classes [9], [10]. An overall service for overcommit ratios, a universal spare capacity table, and a predicting system that is consulted on the internet. We have achieved high availability of each. In a synchronous read path, what they do is transform a regional issue into a global one. Background Overcommitment reports more allocated resources than what is physical capacity, as at the time users do not fully use up all of their resources. Kubernetes puts this out there in requests versus limits and evicts BestEffort and Burstable pods first under node pressure [10]. Large-scale operators use usage forecasts to determine the overcommit ratio; Bashir et al. reported that overcommit, which is based on predicted peak machine use, increased usable CPU capacity by 10- 16 percentage points as compared to no overcommitment [15]. Protean reports that a VM allocator may make decisions in milliseconds by caching machine state instead of asking for it per request [14]. Static stability is when a system maintains its state upon impairment of a dependency [3]. Also, we note that data planes should not depend on control planes to function [4]. In cell-based architecture, the range of impact is reduced by breaking a workload into independent replicas [6]. Problem Analysis Such a service should be able to evaluate the sizes of the tenant quotas, the pool capacity, as well as proper overload situations based on the incoming requests. The ratio and headroom are assumed to be in a global store, which is read in sync. Availability goes up. We hit 99.99% in the regional stack, but the global element only does 99.95%, which in turn pulls the total out to about 99.94%. The end of global dependence indicates that the whole world will face the consequences at the same time. We hit 99.99% in regional availability, but…

articles.title: Why ROUGE Lies About Your LLM Outlines and How Grounded Fine-Tuning Fixes It
articles.content: Key Takeaways The outline should be handled as structured model output: a title paired with paragraph IDs, rather than as text. That small shift makes it machine-checkable for grounding. The hybrid labeling should be compared to an extractive-only and to a generative-only labeling on the same held-out data set when possible; the current version of Table 3 summarizes evidence from the literature rather than gives us results of this comparison. Noisy span boundaries require data-quality checks; without the audit-trail experiment, comparisons of model size should be treated as hypotheses rather than facts. Evaluate in layers: The structural and basic analysis, rubric, and human review. We will do comparisons using ROUGE and BLEU against a single human reference, which is to put forth penalties to the correct paraphrase, which in turn will rank the faulty in terms of structure. Release a measure like (for example, share of documents with acceptable outlines) and report next to the results the human-audited share. Average token overlap is not a release metric. Executive Summary Creating a draft for an extensive unstructured document might initially seem like just summarizing the primary points as a very difficult task. However, it is essentially a structured prediction problem. Each of the elements should refer to specific sections of the text; the draft should contain everything there is in the documents with no information missing or repeated; and the headings should be short, similar in structure and content. In this paper, we will describe a supervised fine-tuning (SFT) approach which uses paragraph IDs as a common basis for tying labels, model output, and assessment. We generate training labels based on extractive candidates and generative rewording, we reject those that do not meet relevance requirements prior to initiating the training stage, and we utilize various assessors connecting evaluation results with acquisition by the reader. Also, we present cases where n-gram metrics fail us and report on the use of prompted models. Introduction Most teams start by prompting. Asking a general-purpose model to "generate a table of contents" produces plausible results quickly, but three problems grow with scale. Titles mention content the section does not contain. Sections go out of order or repeat. The output format varies between each run. We see this type of issue often reported out there [1] also at NIST they put forth confabulation as a unique generative AI risk [2]. Fine-tuning is what usually follows. SFT of curated sets of examples did, in fact, change model action[3, 4]; also, we see small sets of high-quality data may be enough[5]. Training is typically the issue. The hard part is in defining the target and the evaluator, which in turn produces a better outcome. This article looks at those two elements and puts forth a reproducible SFT pipeline for structured outline generation. Background Extractive versus abstractive generation. The extractive method does well in accuracy but at times reports odd results. See et al. showed that a pointer-generator model, which can copy from the source as well as generate, reduced factual errors and repetition compared with a purely abstractive baseline on news summarization [6]. We apply the same idea to label construction rather than to the model architecture. Segmentation. Deciding where sections begin can be learned with supervision [7]. In one part of an outline it is possible to use one title, whilst in an adjacent segment a completely different title is necessary. Attribution. The AIS framework [8] and citation benchmarks [9] turn "is this supported by an identified source?" into a question that can be answered. Paragraph IDs make the source explicit for every outline entry. Problem Analysis A production outline generator has to work within the confines of what a single quality metric includes. articles.title: OData at Scale: When to Use CDS Views, RAP, or API Business Hub in Hybrid SAP
articles.content: Key Takeaways ● CDS (Custom Transactional Services) views for OData exposure, custom RAP-based services, and SAP API Business Hub published APIs present solutions to different problems that, in a mature environment, should be used together rather than one being the default. ● By transaction complexity, we mean RAP for anything beyond CRUD; by consumer type, we mean CDS views for read-heavy Fiori and analytical use; and finally, by governance, we mean API Business Hub for when an external party is involved. ● Select/filter/$batch tuning changes when traffic passes through the Cloud Connector. For a remote BTP extension, metadata caching and the size of $expand responses usually matter more than they do for a Fiori app running alongside the backend. ● With principal propagation through the SAP Cloud Connector and short-lived X.509 certificates, the hybrid setup can apply backend permissions to each end user rather than routing everyone through one shared technical user. ● A CDS which begins as a single internal read view within a few months transforms into a multi-consumer integration point -- we have to go back to the governance and write capability questions in the decision framework instead of asking them once. Executive Summary How do we approach the design of OData for use in Fiori apps, BTP hosted extensions, and third-party integrations? We often see that presenting OData as a one-size-fits-all solution results in services that either do too much for simple read functions or not enough to support business transaction logic. This article presents a decision framework that puts forward three strategies: CDS view-based exposure, custom RESTful ABAP Programming (RAP) services, and SAP API Business Hub published APIs, and ties the choice of strategy to data volatility, consumer type, and governance requirements. Also, we look at the issues of security, performance, and operation that present themselves once the service crosses the on-premises/cloud boundary, and we end with what we learned from putting these services into live hybrid environments. Introduction Most SAP environments are a mix of on-premises and cloud, with an S/4HANA core on-premises that is extended by BTP hosted apps, Fiori launchpads, and non-SAP integrations, and in almost all cases the consumer is reaching the core via OData service [1]. Exposing it as OData is out to be a single decision, which in fact is three separate decisions in the same protocol. We have a CDS view for OData, a custom RAP-based business object, and an API published through API Business Hub, which are for different purposes and fail in different ways under load. A single broad-brush approach applied to all produces either very complex logic for what is really a simple read view, or a thin CDS-based service which tries to do transactional behavior that it was not designed for. Also in hybrid environments we see that a service which is quick for a Fiori app on the ABAP server’s network does better than when the consumer is a BTP extension which uses the Cloud Connector. Latency, security boundaries, and data volatility all change shape at that crossing. What follows is a decision framework for choosing among the three strategies — not a tutorial on building a CDS view or a RAP business object, the latter of which is already well documented in SAP's own developer resources [2], [3]. Background OData is an OASIS/ISO standard for REST-based data services, defining query syntax, a metadata/entity-data-model format, and CRUD/function-invocation conventions over HTTP [1], [4]. SAP uses OData (v2 and, increasingly, v4) as the primary protocol connecting Fiori/UI5, BTP extensions, and external integrations to SAP data. Within an ABAP-based S/4HANA system, there are two structurally different ways to build an OData service: ● CDS-view-based exposure: a CDS view — a database-view-like artifact with declarative annotations for associations, aggregations, and UI metadata — is marked for OData…

articles.title: Another View on Context Parallel for LLMs: Balancing Compute
articles.content: Context Parallelism (CP) splits a batch along the sequence-length dimension, allowing each CP rank to process only a chunk of the original sequence and reducing the memory required for training. I use CP to mean any technique that splits the context length and processes it independently, without relying on Tensor Parallelism, to clearly distinguish Sequence Parallelism from Context Parallelism. Two of my favorite resources motivate CP in terms of long sequences. stas00/ml-engineering : Self-Attention, which is the key component of Transformers, suffers from quadratic memory requirements with respect to the sequence length, therefore when sequence length gets to a certain length, even a batch size of 1 might not be able to fit onto a single GPU and require additional partitioning along the sequence dimension. And once this is done, the sequence can be of any length. The Ultra-Scale Playbook : Context Parallelism (CP) specifically targets the challenge of training with very long sequences by sharding activations along the sequence dimension across GPUs. […] CP is particularly valuable when scaling to extreme sequence lengths (128k+ tokens) where, even when using full activation recomputation, the memory requirements for attention would be prohibitive on a single GPU. That is all true, but CP has another substantial benefit: it can balance attention compute across Data Parallel ranks and improve end-to-end training time by reducing the variance of Flash Attention execution time. Theorem For a fixed global token batch, increasing the Context Parallel degree together with the micro-batch size reduces the variance of Flash Attention execution time. Ignoring communication overhead, the variance decreases proportionally to 1 / CP The benefit comes from keeping the global batch size fixed. As CP increases, the number of DP groups decreases, so each remaining group processes proportionally more independent samples. Their attention costs are averaged across CP ranks, reducing variation. Let’s try to prove this in this article! We will have a computational simulation and a benchmark with a real Flash Attention 3 kernel on an H100. Load balancing is important. In distributed training, iteration time is determined by the slowest rank. Even with Tensor, Pipeline, or Context Parallelism, gradients eventually have to be synchronized across Data Parallel groups. If one group reaches an all-gather or reduce-scatter later than the others, everybody else waits. Stragglers can arise from anywhere: a throttled GPU, a slow network link, or a compute imbalance. Most blocks in a standard transformer scale linearly with sequence length, but attention remains quadratic. Consequently, even small fluctuations in sample length can create severe timing differences across ranks. Ulysses DeepSpeed Ulysses is one of the most widely adopted CP algorithms. It starts with the sequence split into CP equal-sized chunks. Before attention, an all-to-all changes the layout from sequence-sharded to head-sharded: each rank receives the full sequence for a subset of attention heads. A reverse all-to-all restores the sequence-sharded layout afterward. This reduces per-rank activation memory by a factor of CP , although the exact reduction depends on the attention architecture. With GQA, KV heads may need to be replicated once CP exceeds the number of KV heads. We assume independent samples drawn from a length distribution. As CP increases, we increase the micro-batch size (and hence the token budget of each remaining group) so the global batch remains fixed: (N / CP) · (CP · S) = N · S . articles.title: 6 Scenes, 36 Store Screenshots: A Fixture Pipeline for Identical iOS and Android Listings
articles.content: How fixture data, UI tests, and Pillow turn six app scenes into matching store images across phones, tablets, and foldables Our courier app's screenshots need to look identical on iOS and Android. If a delivery appears on a phone or a tablet, it should have the same caption, same progress and same messages. To make that happen, we developed a pipeline that opens up six scenes with placeholder data, takes screenshots of them on emulators and simulators, and then adds a caption with Pillow. Our configured set covers three devices per platform, producing 18 App Store images and 18 Play Store images. Capturing and adding a caption are separate steps. So we could change a headline without having to restart the app. One fictional morning at 9:41 What's nice about this approach is that each screenshot depends so little on a live account. The app provides predictable data; the test opens a known scene; and the compositor provides presentation. In the code below, for simplicity, I've removed project-specific wiring and names. Each screenshot follows the day of a fictional courier, Maya, in the San Francisco Bay Area. She makes a pickup of a lab specimen, runs an errand for aircraft parts and exchanges a message with dispatch. On each platform, the scenes use a fixtures file containing the same orders. The fixture clock is anchored to 9:41 on the day of the capture. In the status bar we see 9:41, so "picked up at 9:37" and "arriving in 10 minutes" make sense in every screenshot. The addresses are of real businesses. The people are fictional. iOS: a DEBUG launch argument and deeplink routing On iOS, to enter screenshot mode, you pass a launch argument. Only DEBUG builds of the app include this argument. If you pass it, the app swaps out its auth session and service container for fixture versions. Writes to the app have no effect. Reads will return data from the fixtures. Analytics are disabled and first-run cards are automatically dismissed. Another argument picks which scene to open. And via the same flow used by Live Activities and push notifications, that scene is opened: #if DEBUG enum ScreenshotMode { static let isEnabled = ProcessInfo.processInfo.arguments.contains("-ScreenshotMode") static let scene: ScreenshotScene? = { let args = ProcessInfo.processInfo.arguments guard isEnabled, let i = args.firstIndex(of: "-ScreenshotScene"), args.indices.contains(i + 1) else { return nil } return ScreenshotScene(rawValue: args[i + 1]) }() } enum ScreenshotScene: String { case orders, orderStops, orderMessages @MainActor func apply(to router: DeeplinkRouter) { switch self { case .orders: router.selectedTab = .orders case .orderStops: router.open(.order(id: Fixtures.specimenOrderId, tab: .stops)) case .orderMessages: router.open(.order(id: Fixtures.specimenOrderId, tab: .messages)) } } } #endif No tap is needed in the app to open up a scene. So each screenshot is reproducible. In screenshot mode, even screens deeper than a route (e.g. a proof of delivery checklist) will have their selection seeded. These tests check is that a scene appeared. It's up to interaction tests to tap through to it. Each scene is one XCUITest, which takes a scene argument, waits for a fixture string and then calls snapshot("order-stops") . With this in mind, fastlane snapshot fires off these tests in each simulator. It uses a 9:41 status bar and en-US locale. A Python script spins up simulators (on the latest runtime) for each device. It sets GPS on the driver fixture, and pre-approves location. That way, we won't pick up a prompt in any capture. In our iOS pipeline, we have lanes for the phone/tablet set and for the foldable set. And it matters which comes first. bundle exec fastlane screenshots bundle exec fastlane screenshots_duo Each lane is in our project. It depends on our capture tests, setup of simulators and use of fixtures. Android: a separate build type On Android, our fixtures live in a build type of screenshots , with its own source set . articles.title: What Marketing Trends Will Dominate the Next Five Years?
articles.content: In an era of unimaginable communication clutter where brands are struggling desperately to establish their presence, it is not at all easy to predict what marketing trends to watch out for in the coming five years. While AI continues to dominate everybody's consciousness, equally striking fear and hope in the hearts and minds of marketers and brand managers, marketing itself is evolving in fundamental ways. There is a subtle yet very perceptible shift in the way that people relate to and engage with brands, and marketers need to speak to that. Gaining their target audience’s trust will become increasingly important in a world where AI-generated content will make a surfeit of information available to whoever seeks it in an instant. Learning about and engaging with customers at an individual level will be the way to influence them. 1. AI will be integral to marketing. The efficiencies that AI imparts to the marketing process will ensure that it becomes an integral part of the latter. With content creation and campaign management being largely handed over to AI, marketers and brand managers will be able to focus on core strategising and helping brands differentiate themselves in the market. Importantly, autonomous agents are all set to change the very paradigm of marketing thanks to their ability to liaise between customers and brands on account of their being able to automate both shopping decisions and campaign execution. 2. SEO alongside GEO & AEO. The way people search online has changed with conversational AI involving both research and recommendation in place of the search listings of old, increasingly becoming the norm. In the time ahead, one will likely see SEO coexisting with Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) and Answer Engine Optimization (AEO). This will help one obtain access to well-structured and pertinent content providing specific answers to queries, which will naturally carry enhanced credibility. Brands will earn greater respectability with this kind of content, especially if it gets cited by credible publications. According to BCG, the incidence of research-backed buyer journeys is going up, even as the impediments in carrying out exhaustive research are reduced. 3. Social Media will be about Relationships rather than just reach. The present-day obsession with the number of connections and virality will give way to cultivating niche communities and professional networks and conversations initiated by creators. Investing in building sustained conversations with those that really matter will be the cornerstone of the new social media approach followed by brands. Follower count and the number of impressions will matter less than meaningful engagements that lead to a sense of community and participation. 4. Personalization will mean speaking to individual needs rather than marketing segments In the days ahead, marketers will be able to move from personalising their offerings for marketing segments to being able to cater to the specific needs of individuals. Using AI will help them come up with bespoke product recommendations, tailored product journeys as well as personalised service interactions. What's more, it will be common for AI agents to help prospects both make product comparisons and regular transactions, with all of this happening at scale. At the same time, extreme care will have to be taken to prevent the process from becoming intrusive in any manner. 5. Influencer marketing will have to prove its worth. Influencer marketing is not going anywhere in the next few years, but its current dream run will end. It will have to prove its worth in an era of AI-generated content and synthetic personalities, where influencers will have to prove their credibility for brands to take them seriously. Subject matter mastery and demonstrable expertise would be the deciding factors here. According to a 2026 Gartner marketing survey , 35% of consumers already rely less on influencers on account of AI. This possibly…

articles.title: Amazon Puts a Camera In Its Echo Studio So Alexa Can See
articles.content: Amazon has added a camera to its Echo Studio speaker, allowing Alexa to visually identify objects, help with tasks and remotely monitor a room. For those concerned about privacy, Amazon is keeping a camera-free version available. The Next Web reports: The camera speaker ships today for $249.99. Hold up a board game box and Alexa can explain the rules, or show it a box of cereal and it can help you reorder it, according to Amazon. Owners can also check in on the room from the Alexa app while they are away. The Echo Studio without a camera stays on sale at $219.99. A dedicated button turns off the microphones and any camera, and a visual indicator shows when a camera streams images or video to the cloud, Amazon said. Certain features require Alexa+, which is included with a Prime membership. Other devices Amazon unveiled today include an Echo Time alarm clock, an Alexa Photo Frame and the Echo Show 16. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
