articles.title: MiniMax Open-Sources MCode Stack: 15 Agent Skills Its Coding Team Uses Daily
articles.content: MiniMax has open-sourced MCode Stack , the workflows and agent skills its team uses to build MiniMax Code. The MiniMax MCode Stack agent skills went public on October 28, 2026 under the MIT license . It is not a prompt collection. Each piece is a SKILL.md skill or checklist that installs directly into MiniMax Code . For developers, it turns harness engineering habits into steps an agent can actually run. TL;DR Size: 2 stacks, 17 skills (15 from Ronny, 2 from Jiachen), 5 checklists, 5 companion notes. Runs on: Any machine running MiniMax Code (Node.js 22.19+) or Claude Code. No GPU. Skills are plain Markdown. Performance: No benchmarks or eval results published. Best: long-command-check , a 10-point audit for long shell commands and background tasks. We just open-sourced MCode Stack: the actual workflows and skills the MiniMax Code team uses every day to build MiniMax Code. https://t.co/vREt7i8m2M — RonnyHe (@Ronny_MiniMax) October 28, 2026 What is MiniMax MCode Stack? MCode Stack is an open-source repo of agent skills from MiniMax’s MiniMax Code team. MiniMax Code is the MiniMax’s open-source terminal coding agent, also MIT-licensed. The stack holds no MiniMax Code source code. It holds only workflows, skills and checklists. The repo pairs with a column called MCode Engineering Notes . Each note explains one idea. The repo makes that idea runnable. Published notes cover subagents , tool context , compaction versus memory and long bash commands . A note on per-turn context tax is marked upcoming. What skills are inside Ronny’s stack? MiniMax’s stack ships 15 skills, grouped by moment in the working day: Plan and split (3): subagent-split-check , engineering-small-prs , engineering-change-descriptions . Context and tools (2): tool-budget-audit , context-tax-audit . Long sessions and commands (3): long-session-check , handoff-doc , long-command-check . Review (4): independent-review , engineering-code-review , engineering-review-comments , engineering-review-feedback . Experiments and hotfixes (3): harness-experiment , trajectory-review , engineering-emergency-changes . A few ideas stand out. independent-review gives the reviewer exactly 3 inputs: the diff, the requirement and test results. It deliberately withholds the author’s conversation. The reasoning: a reviewer inheriting the author’s context repeats the author’s blind spots. subagent-split-check says to split work only when context is the measured problem. Splitting by team or question type is not a valid reason. tool-budget-audit separates 2 costs: tool definitions and tool results. Tool search mainly cuts the first. Programmatic tool calling mainly cuts the second. harness-experiment enforces 1 change per experiment. It tracks flipped tasks, requests per task, tokens, cache hit rate and wall-clock time. The long-command checklist has 10 items. It asks whether moving a command to background re-runs the process. It also asks whether unread results survive compaction. The 6 engineering-* skills are adapted from Google Engineering Practices . That material stays under CC-BY 3.0, per the stack’s NOTICE . How do you install MCode Stack? There are 3 paths, per the README : One skill: clone the repo and copy a skill folder into ~/.agents/skills/ . Whole stack as a local plugin: copy stacks/ronny into MiniMax Code’s local plugin directory. Marketplace: in MiniMax Code desktop, add the MiniMax-AI/mcode-stack marketplace. This option is rolling out gradually. The same catalog works in Claude Code with /plugin marketplace add MiniMax-AI/mcode-stack . MiniMax Code also reads ~/.claude/skills/ and ~/.codex/skills/ . The skills use the common SKILL.md format, so most work in other agents that support skills. How does MCode Stack compare with other skill packs? articles.title: Apple launches new MacBook Pro with touchscreen and OLED — starts at $2,899
articles.content: Apple finally has touchscreen laptops. At an event in Los Angeles, the company detailed its new MacBook Pros featuring OLED XDR displays that you can control with your fingers. The 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pros are available for pre-order now and will ship on Nov. 6. The 14-incher will start at $2,899, while the 16-incher will start at $3,399. The systems use Apple's existing M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, and go up to 16TB of storage and 128GB of memory. These systems also feature the first redesigns for the MacBook Pro since 2021, when the M1 Pro and M1 Max launched in what has become a familiar design with a notch. These new models include the Dynamic Island around the webcam, similar to the iPhone, which can be used for real-time notifications. They also have light-up Apple logos, which we haven't seen on a MacBook Pro since 2016. The PROLED XDR display comes in 14.2-and 16.3-inch sizes, with ProMotion allowing for refresh rates between 10 Hz and 120 Hz. Apple claims 2,000 nits of peak brightness and a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio for intensely deep blacks. (Image credit: Apple) The 14-inch MacBook Pro is 3 pounds, about half a pound less than the existing version, while the 16-inch MacBook Pro is 4 pounds, or 0.7 pounds lighter than it was before. Apple's bezels are also less noticeable than before. The hinge seems to be a point of pride (that's the second time this month, after the iPhone Duo). In this case, it's that the screen is less prone to wobble when you touch it. The new laptops are only slightly thinner than their predecessor. Apple claims that the 16-inch model is "nearly a millimeter thinner" and the 14-incher is "half a millimeter thinner." Apple attributes those shavings to OLED's display stack. (Image credit: Apple) Apple's own apps are already set to work with touch out of the box, and the company says many other apps will already work right away, including Notion, Canva, Zoom, Microsoft Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Adobe Lightroom, DaVinci Resolve, Blender, and more. Apple already had the best speakers in a laptop, and now it's promising improvements: 50% deeper bass and new tweeters for clearer sound. There's even dedicated audio tuning for people who want to use the speakers with their laptop lid closed. The significant change to the Mac is another in a flurry of launches for new CEO John Ternus, who also recently introduced the iPhone 18 Pro; the foldable iPhone Duo; Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4; HomeView; and a new iPad Mini, also with an OLED panel. The devices follow a long resistance to touchscreen laptops from Apple. Former CEO Steve Jobs, at an event introducing Mac OS X Lion in 2010, called laptops with touchscreens "ergonomically terrible" , claiming that "after an extended period of time, your arm wants to fall off." (HomeView, Apple's smart home manager, has a vertical touchscreen and no one has made a peep about that. The iPad, too, has been vertical on Apple's keyboards, though some of those include touchpads as well). The Mac resisted a touchscreen throughout former CEO Tim Cook's tenure, as well, though these new laptops definitely were developed under his leadership. In the last decade, touchscreens have become a common feature on laptops running Windows, and Microsoft's latest operating system, Windows 11, was designed to be slightly more touch-friendly than its predecessors.

articles.title: Malaysia seizes $12 million worth of advanced AI chips hidden inside 30 servers
articles.content: Malaysian customs have seized over $12 million (49.5 million Malaysian ringgit) worth of advanced AI chips in a single bust, as the country clamps down on a suspected semiconductor smuggling syndicate. According to a Reuters report on October 28 , officials found 30 servers containing the chips at Kuala Lumpur International Airport’s free trade zone on October 15th. Initial investigations revealed that the shipment originated in an Asian country and was bound for another undisclosed Asian country. Go deeper with TH Premium: AI and data centers (Image credit: Microsoft) The data center cooling state of play The custom AI ASIC state of play America’s AI chip rules keep changing — and the rest of the world is paying the price GTC 2026: Ian Buck press Q&A transcript — VP of Hyperscale and HPC speaks out on shelving CPX and shipping LPU decode this year Demand for data center CPUs has surged, and AI agents are responsible The airport’s customs director, Aspalila Ag Tuah, confirmed that the servers were falsely declared as ordinary electronic goods, saying the suspected scheme used Malaysia as a transit point to avoid restrictions on the goods’ onward movement. The Malaysian company involved in the shipment has been summoned to assist in the investigation. Authorities suspect that the foiled smuggling attempt was carried out by the same group responsible for a similar attempt last June. On June 5, customs officers discovered 72 server units containing advanced AI chips at the Kuala Lumpur International Airport, valued at approximately $13 million. This shipment had also been falsely declared as computer components and was meant to be reshipped without the required permit. Aspalila said the network has been linked to seizures worth over $25 million so far across at least five cases. She declined to provide further information on the network or the current case, citing ongoing investigations. Several key facts remain unknown, including the chip type, country of manufacture, final destination, and intended recipient — whether a company or a military organization. The U.S. had placed export controls on the movement of advanced Nvidia and other U.S.-origin AI chips to China , the most likely destination for the seized chips. Smuggling networks began using Malaysia, a U.S. ally not affected by the controls, as a hub, exporting the banned chips to the country before re-exporting them to China. While the country’s geographic location and mature logistics infrastructure make it important for legitimate international trade, these characteristics also make it ideal for smuggling sensitive technology. To restrict this avenue, Malaysia subsequently imposed export controls on the ​movement of advanced AI chips of U.S. origin , at Washington’s request. Other Asian U.S. allies, such as Singapore and Taiwan, have implemented similar controls. Demand for powerful Nvidia GPUs remains high in China, fueling a booming market for smuggled hardware .
articles.author: Etiido Uko

articles.title: Former T-Mobile CEO Mike Sievert exits board of directors, wraps up his run at the wireless giant
articles.content: Mike Sievert in 2017 when he was serving as T-Mobile’s COO before rising to CEO in 2020. (GeekWire File Photo/Kevin Lisota) Former T-Mobile CEO Mike Sievert is hanging up his magenta hat, leaving the wireless giant’s board of directors and vice chair role effective Nov. 1. Sievert will also leave the board’s Transaction Committee, according to a federal filing. His departure comes a year after he handed the CEO job to Srini Gopalan . A company spokesperson said via email that the vice chair role was structured as a one-year term, adding that Sievert has “been a valued strategic advisor throughout the leadership transition, and we’re incredibly grateful for his contributions.” T-Mobile said in the filing that his departure “is not the result of any disagreement with the Company on any matter relating to its operations, policies or practices.” Sievert joined T-Mobile in 2012 as executive vice president and chief marketing officer, the same year John Legere became CEO. He later became president and chief operating officer and was mentored by Legere before succeeding him as chief executive in 2020. He served as CEO for about five and a half years. Sievert was a central figure in T-Mobile’s campaign to brand itself the “Un-carrier.” During his time at the company, T-Mobile grew from fewer than 30 million customers to more than 130 million by September 2025, a period that included its merger with Sprint. Once the scrappy outsider, Bellevue, Wash.-based T-Mobile currently ranks second among U.S. telecom companies by market capitalization, behind Verizon and ahead of AT&T. Sievert previously worked at Microsoft, AT&T Wireless, E-Trade, IBM and Procter & Gamble.

articles.title: Amazon tells tokenmaxxing devs to slow their AI roll
articles.content: Maximize value, not token usage, Amazon has told its engineers, citing concerns about rising AI costs and complexity. Amazon made the strategy shift public on Tuesday in a note to engineering teams outlining the changing role of its software development engineers in the age of AI. “Our most prolific engineers have demonstrated that neither the developer role nor their output is defined by the use of AI,” Amazon VP and distinguished engineer Terk Terkowitz wrote in the note. “We're now in the era of the Renaissance Developer, blending AI tools with human judgment and domain expertise to build entirely new things.” In other words, Amazon wants its developers using AI, but burning through tokens isn't the same thing as getting useful work done. Rather than define the developer role by how AI is used, the memo focuses on what isn't changing so fast: the need to deliver useful software and results for customers and the business. “It is difficult to define, in a way that will stand the test of time, what good AI powered engineering practices look like,” the memo continues. “We have decided to focus on what is not changing as we evolved the SDE roles … the outcomes that matter aren’t changing, even if the inputs, tools, and techniques are changing faster than ever.” What that means for software developers in the present moment is that AI input metrics, even if Amazon has seen some correlation with increased productivity and delivery on tokenmaxxing teams, aren’t what Amazon sees as a measurement of good use of developer time and resources. “We are all aware of how deeply flawed these metrics are, primarily because they are disconnected from what matters,” the memo argues. “[U]sing these metrics could, if used as a target instead of a measure, drive negative outcomes, increasing costs, and increasing complexity,” the memo continues, referring to tokenmaxxing costs and overly complex code that’s at odds with Amazon’s mission to “invent and simplify.” An Amazon spokesperson confirmed that the memo’s intent was to discourage tokenmaxxing, pointing us to comments from AWS CEO Matt Garman from June in which he encouraged developers to measure outcomes, not token consumption, in making proper use of AI tools for software development. Amazon also wants its developers thinking more about how AI can help “improve delivery for customers” and business units, not just trying to find a place to stick it to prove it's working for them. The memo calls out some engineering teams who’ve “become less connected to their customers and business,” and says teams that are more engaged with their products and business roles “are able to take the most advantage of AI and agentic software development,” in essence calling for more teams to take a similar approach. “If your work does not benefit from current AI tooling, that is a finding, not a failing,” the memo said. “An engineer who can explain where AI does not yet help their work is demonstrating the judgement we are asking for.” Amazon's take in the memo is starkly similar to what Microsoft told its own internal development teams in August, right down to stressing a focus on returns for customers and business instead of maximizing input. "Tokenmaxxing is not what we are optimizing for," Microsoft EVP Jay Parikh told developers. "I want all of us focused on maximizing outcomes that move the needle for our customers and our business." With that, the writing seems to be on the wall for the throw-AI-at-everything-and-see-where-it-sticks approach to integrating the tech. When two companies that large start to question whether AI token consumption is a useful measure of productivity for their thousands of software engineers, it's possible the rest of the world will soon start sipping those tokens instead of chugging them. That, or we'll soon see even more enterprises begin to embrace the philosophy of relying on "good enough" open-weight models that can handle many tasks at a fraction of the cost of more…
articles.author: Brandon Vigliarolo

articles.title: The Accent-Stripping One-Liner Broke Our Search Results in Korean
articles.content: Stack Overflow’s top accent fix changes string length, so for three months we cut Korean snippets in the wrong place. Search found the word. The preview was cut somewhere else. Credit: Image generated with ChatGPT In July we made our search accent-insensitive. Type “skoda” and you find “Škoda”. Type “cafe” and you find “café”. It took one line, the same line most JavaScript developers reach for, and it fixed search for every user writing in French, Czech, Polish or Vietnamese. For the next three months, that line also meant a Korean user searching their chat history got results whose preview did not contain the word they searched for. Sometimes the preview was just “…”. The search was right. The preview was cut in the wrong place. I co-founded AI Toolbox, a Chrome extension used by 40,000 people that adds full-text search to ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and Grok. Each search result shows a snippet: a short window of the message with your word in the middle. This is the story of how a famous one-liner broke that window for Korean and Japanese text, why our tests never noticed, and the small change that fixed it. The One-Liner Everyone Copies The Stack Overflow question “Remove accents/diacritics in a string in JavaScript” had been viewed 592,224 times as of October 2026. Its top answer, at a score of 2,101, is this: const str = "Crème Brûlée" str.normalize("NFD").replace(/[̀-ͯ]/g, "") > "Creme Brulee" normalize("NFD") splits a precomposed letter into a base letter plus a combining mark, so "è" becomes "e" followed by U+0300. The regular expression then deletes every mark in the range U+0300 to U+036F. Our version lowercased first and mapped a few atomic letters such as "ł" and "ø", and we ran it on both the query and the text, so "skoda" and "Škoda" both became "skoda". The answer is correct for what it was asked: comparing strings. The bug came from what we did next. To build a snippet, we found the match in the folded text and then cut the original text at the same position. Our own comment said why that was safe: “the folded string keeps the SAME length and the SAME character offsets as the lowercased original. That length-preservation is deliberately relied on by the snippet/highlight code” And it said why other scripts were not at risk: “Non-Latin scripts (CJK, Arabic, Hebrew, Cyrillic) carry no combining marks to strip and pass through unchanged” Both sentences were wrong. Here is the snippet code from our Gemini module, as it shipped in July: export function getContextSnippet(content: string, query: string, contextChars: number = 58): string { // Accent-folded, length-preserving lookup: an accent-insensitive query still // centres the snippet on the match, and the offset is valid on the original. const matchIndex = foldAccents(content).indexOf(foldAccents(query)); if (matchIndex === -1) return content.substring(0, contextChars * 2); const start = Math.max(0, matchIndex - contextChars); const end = Math.min(content.length, matchIndex + query.length + contextChars); let snippet = content.substring(start, end); matchIndex comes from one string. content.substring cuts another. The ChatGPT, Claude, Grok and cross-app search modules each had their own copy of the same pattern, five in all. What NFD Actually Does to Korean NFD does not only split accented Latin letters. It decomposes anything that has a canonical decomposition, and the regular expression only removes marks in one block. Every Korean syllable decomposes. “한” becomes three jamo, U+1112 U+1161 U+11AB. “가” becomes two. The Unicode normalization report, UAX #15 , notes that “the decompositions and compositions for Hangul syllables are algorithmic”: a syllable splits into two jamo, or three when it has a final consonant. None of those jamo are in U+0300 to U+036F, so the regular expression keeps all of them. Japanese voiced kana do the same thing. “が” becomes “か” plus U+3099, and “パ” becomes “ハ” plus U+309A. Arabic alef with madda, “آ”, becomes alef plus U+0653. Even…

articles.title: MPF Mapping: A Myelin Readout From Routine Brain MRI
articles.content: AI-assistance disclosure: I drafted this article with AI assistance, then edited it and fact-checked every number against the paper (arXiv:2610.37213). A self-supervised network turns T1w, T2w and FLAIR scans into macromolecular pool fraction maps, with public code and weights. Most brain MRI archives are full of T1-weighted, T2-weighted and FLAIR scans, and almost none of them contain a quantitative myelin measurement. Getting one usually means adding a dedicated quantitative magnetization transfer (qMT) sequence, which costs scan time and only helps for patients scanned after you add it. Jelmer van Lune, Miha Fuderer, Oscar van der Heide, Matteo Maspero, Martin B. Schilder, Jan Willem Dankbaar, Stefano Mandija and Alessandro Sbrizzi at UMC Utrecht estimate the macromolecular pool fraction (MPF), a myelin-sensitive biomarker, straight from those three routine contrasts. The method is described in arXiv:2610.37213 , and the PyTorch code and trained weights are on GitHub. What MPF is, in one paragraph In a two-pool model of brain tissue, part of the protons sit in free water and part are bound to macromolecules such as proteins and lipids. The bound protons relax far too fast to image directly, but they trade magnetization with the free water and change how fast the visible signal recovers. MPF is the fraction of protons in that bound pool. Myelin carries a lot of it, so MPF is lower where myelin is lost, and post-mortem work has tied reduced MPF to histological demyelination. MS studies use it for exactly that reason. Why a clinic or viewer team should care The input is the protocol most sites already run: a 3D T1w (spoiled gradient echo or MPRAGE), an axial 2D T2w turbo spin echo and a 3D FLAIR. The output is an MPF map, plus free-water T1, T2 and proton density maps, for every past and future session that has those scans. For a research archive that means retrospective myelin studies on thousands of patients without recalling anyone. For a viewer or PACS add-on, it is one more parametric overlay you can compute in the background and show next to FLAIR, the way the paper does in Figure 3. Pipeline builders hit one catch: the physics model needs the acquisition parameters of each scan: TR, TE, TI, flip angle and the sequence-averaged RF power, B1rms. The authors pulled these from DICOM headers for the Utrecht data and from metadata files for the public set. B1rms has its own DICOM attribute (0018,1320), but anonymization tools and NIfTI conversions often drop it, so keep the original headers or a sidecar file. How the method works A 2D U-Net reads all three contrasts. A shared encoder processes T1w, T2w and FLAIR slices separately, attention modules fuse the features at each level, and one decoder outputs four maps: free-water T1, free-water T2, proton density and MPF. The network has 9.06 million trainable parameters and works on 224 x 224 axial slices. The scanner settings steer the network. Each contrast comes with a nine-value vector (contrast type, log TR, log TE, sine of the flip angle, B1rms, inversion flag, log TI). A small MLP turns it into an embedding that drives adaptive instance normalization in the encoder, so the same weights read a Philips spoiled GRE and a Siemens MPRAGE differently. Training needs no reference maps. The predicted maps go through closed-form Bloch signal equations for each sequence type, with a magnetization transfer term that links apparent T1 to MPF and to the sequence’s RF power. The loss compares the synthesized T1w, T2w and FLAIR images with the acquired ones. Because free-water T1 and MPF can trade off against each other, a prior on white matter T1 and a soft lower bound on proton density keep the solution in a physical range. Training ran for 20 epochs on 6,084 sessions and took about 12 hours on a single NVIDIA RTX 4500 Ada GPU. articles.title: GitHub powering up four million extra cores to stop its service going down
articles.content: GitHub's Universe conference kicked off in San Francisco on Wednesday with news that its infrastructural universe is expanding to address staggering demand from AI agents. GitHub recorded 7.4 billion code commits in September 2026, five times more than hit its servers a year earlier. This surge in traffic over the past year, the result of developers running AI agents and generating increased amounts of programming code, caught the company unprepared and led to a series of outages and service availability woes. AI-driven code commits started becoming a problem last December, and led to problems in February , April , August , not to mention the months in between. On May 7, the site's 90-day availability hit a low of about 84 percent , according to reconstructed data from GitHub's status page. GitHub execs apologized and promised to do better. Those commitments have put four million CPU cores and 160 petabytes of high-speed storage on its infrastructure roadmap, alongside extra compute capacity for GitHub Actions, the company's beleaguered continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) platform. The Microsoft-owned code hosting biz also says it is redesigning its technical architecture (an effort discussed previously ) to separate compute and storage, with the expectation that will enable 35x more throughput. "We’re also migrating to a multi-region deployment in Azure , while continuing to serve incredible levels of traffic from developers around the world," said Jay Parikh, EVP of CoreAI, Microsoft, in a blog post provided to The Register . "We expect to complete the migration early next year. Those investments give us more room to grow. The next step is building the systems that handle the work." Also at the its Universe event , GitHub announced general availability of Copilot Fusion, the company's model routing service that was previewed under the name HydraFusion . The idea is that allowing GitHub to route requests to different models can improve task-completion rates while reducing token consumption costs. "Different tasks need different models," said Parikh. "Developers shouldn’t have to manage every model choice to get the right result at the right price. Copilot Fusion evaluates what a task needs across reasoning, code generation, debugging, and tool use, then chooses how to execute across one or more models. In the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, Fusion Max scored within two points of Opus 5.5 Max at half the cost and 40% less time per task." GitHub is making more bells and whistles available through its Copilot app, including Copilot Projects, for coordinating parallel work; Copilot Connectors, for simplifying how Copilot connects to MCP servers; and Copilot Automations, which are reusable agent tasks. And in what appears to be an effort to boost Copilot usage in the workplace, GitHub is extending Copilot access to all GitHub Enterprise users without requiring any additional per-seat purchases. Customer still get billed for the tokens they use. Microsoft's code collab biz is also expanding its suite of AI services for developers with an offering called AI Scans, which checks pull requests for vulnerabilities in languages not addressed by rule-based scanning and in code that's already merged, plus new reachability analysis tools that allow development to focus on issues that are plausibly exploitable. Another new offering is a package firewall that checks enterprise policy settings before fetching npm packages. ®

articles.title: The Crunchbase Tech Layoffs Tracker
articles.content: Methodology This tracker includes layoffs conducted by U.S.-based companies or those with a strong U.S. presence and is updated at least bi-weekly. We’ve included both startups and publicly traded, tech-heavy companies. We’ve also included companies based elsewhere that have a sizable team in the United States, such as Klarna , even when it’s unclear how much of the U.S. workforce has been affected by layoffs. Layoff and workforce figures are best estimates based on reporting. We source the layoffs from media reports, our own reporting, social media posts and layoffs.fyi , a crowdsourced database of tech layoffs. We recently updated our layoffs tracker to reflect the most recent round of layoffs each company has conducted. This allows us to quickly and more accurately track layoff trends, which is why you might notice some changes in our most recent numbers. If an employee headcount cannot be confirmed to our standards, we note it as “unclear.”

articles.title: GitHub debuts Copilot Fusion, a new model selection & orchestration system that beats Claude Code for half the API cost
articles.content: GitHub has debuted GitHub Copilot Fusion , a new system that handles model selection and orchestration for coding tasks so developers don’t have to. Combining the advanced runtime model orchestration from Project HydraFusion with Copilot Auto Model Selection , Copilot Fusion can now handle both model selection and orchestration. GitHub says Fusion Max delivered comparable benchmark performance to Claude Code with Opus 5.5 Max at about half the average API cost and in about 40% less time per task. Generally available now, GitHub Copilot Fusion is part of GitHub’s new vision to make GitHub “the most comprehensive software delivery system in the world,” with developers delegating model choices while retaining responsibility for the direction and outcome of the work. GitHub announced the news on Wednesday at GitHub Universe in San Francisco, the company’s flagship developer event. Copilot Fusion debuted Wednesday at GitHub Universe in San Francisco. (Credit: The New Stack ) GitHub Copilot Fusion is the decider now For tasks involving reasoning, code generation, debugging, or tool use, GitHub says developers can delegate decisions about which models to use and how they work together. Its instructions: “choose Copilot Fusion and let Copilot intelligently route and orchestrate which models it uses for you.” That sounds like a time-saver, since different tasks benefit from different models based on capabilities and cost. With Copilot Fusion working as the “model picker,” developers don’t have to weigh performance and price for every task. More compelling is the idea that developers can use Copilot Fusion to strategically switch models mid-workflow, letting the system jump between models based on what best suits each step. After analyzing what the task requires and choosing a model, the system orchestrates the next steps based on what makes the most sense. That may be a single model doing everything, a “cascading” workflow where a quality check evaluates one model’s response and then decides to accept it or escalate it, or a “critique” workflow where one model reviews another’s work. That could reduce the mental load for developers who may inadvertently choose inefficient models when their attention drifts. As Hari Pokhrel , principal software engineer at AT&T, describes in a statement for GitHub: “Previously, developers would often choose a more powerful model for a complex task and forget to switch back for everyday activities.” So, what do developers get to decide for themselves? Mostly, the effort level. While Copilot Fusion handles model selection and orchestration, developers choose the effort level: Fusion Standard for everyday coding; Fusion High for more challenging tasks and deeper reasoning; Fusion Max for the most demanding, complex work. That’s if you’re free and comfortable letting GitHub’s systems take the lead. If you prefer, developers can implement other controls. Per GitHub, enterprise administrators can control which models Copilot Fusion can choose from, disabling certain models for Copilot Fusion without disabling them for the entire developer team. Administrators can also adjust the policy state for each model independently and set whether Copilot Fusion is or isn’t the default model for Copilot users. Click to enlarge image. (Credit: The New Stack ) The case for letting Copilot Fusion be your guide According to GitHub and Pokhrel’s statement, offloading model selection and orchestration to the new fusion system is the smarter route for developers, letting you balance performance and cost without the friction of choosing between models. GitHub says it has improved performance since launching Project HydraFusion as a research preview in September 2026. articles.title: GitHub saw 7.4B commits in September, adding 4M CPU cores and 160 PB of storage to keep up
articles.content: GitHub is seeing unprecedented demand and is updating its core infrastructure to keep pace. In August, GitHub said it was seeing 2.9 billion commits per month , up from 1.4 billion in April. At its GitHub Universe conference on Wednesday, the company announced that it is now seeing 7.4 billion commits per month. To put that into perspective, developers pushed 65 million monthly commits to the platform in 2024. That kind of growth is a great problem to have, but the company’s outages have become something of a recurring theme. The reason is rapid usage growth, driven mostly by “agentic demand,” as the company puts it. Credit: The New Stack. 4 million more CPU cores In August, GitHub CTO Vlad Fedorov announced that the platform had added 3 million CPU cores — mostly on Azure — to support this growth. Now, GitHub says it has added 4 million CPU cores, plus 160 petabytes of high-speed storage and more compute power for GitHub Actions so far this year The company also added 50 Tb/s of network capacity to keep all of this data flowing. A new GitHub architecture is coming GitHub also used this announcement to reiterate its commitment to rearchitecting its platform to separate compute and storage. It first talked about this earlier this month . At that time, the company noted that its internal benchmarks show that this new architecture can deliver up to 35x higher write throughput, for example. Credit: The New Stack. “Agents are changing the volume and shape of software development. Adding capacity matters, but capacity alone won’t get us there. We’ve also had to change the architecture,” Jay Parikh, the EVP for Core AI at Microsoft, writes in the announcement. Separating compute and storage isn’t exactly radical in 2026, but it shows GitHub was trying to scale on a legacy foundation. Moving to Azure and its services was essentially the only option, especially as the company’s own data center was out of capacity. Credit: The New Stack. The post GitHub saw 7.4B commits in September, adding 4M CPU cores and 160 PB of storage to keep up appeared first on The New Stack .

articles.title: GitHub Universe 2026: Evolving every layer of the stack
articles.content: Our jobs as developers are changing. In a couple of years, we’ve gone from writing every line of code to working with AI assistants to orchestrating fleets of agents. But the goal hasn’t changed: ship completed software work. A feature, a bug fix, a security fix. Completed work, not more code, is the output that matters. Today at GitHub Universe , we shared our vision for GitHub as the most comprehensive software delivery system in the world. We introduced products that bring that vision to life and showed how we’re rebuilding the infrastructure underneath it. Our vision: From idea to completed software The SDLC is no longer a linear path from planning to coding to testing to deployment. A code change, a request from a colleague, or a production metric can trigger work anywhere in the system. Most of us (and our agents) jump between different stages, depending on the task at hand. Developers set the direction, make decisions, and stay accountable for what ships. Agents implement and verify changes. And everything feeds into and out of a continuous learning machine that makes the next cycle better. This agentic software delivery system solves for three things: Velocity: get from idea to completed software as quickly, efficiently, and cost-effectively as possible Intelligence: combine context across the platform with a continuous learning engine, so the system gets better as you use it Quality: make completed work secure by default and catch bugs before they ship GitHub is built for developers and their agents. We’re also making the underlying primitives available, so you can build your own bespoke solutions. You stay in control of the work, the tools, and the cost. New features and products that move the work forward Today at Universe, we showed some of the latest products and features in action, starting with the GitHub Copilot app. GitHub Copilot app: From issue to merge, in one app The GitHub Copilot app is designed from the ground up for agentic software delivery. It connects your agents and tools across projects, so you can direct the work without making every handoff. And it’s for more than producing code: you can write specs, present design discussions, or analyze telemetry in one agent-first surface. Copilot Fusion: Multi-model orchestration at its finest Different tasks need different models. Developers shouldn’t have to manage every model choice to get the right result at the right price. Copilot Fusion evaluates what a task needs across reasoning, code generation, debugging, and tool use, then chooses how to execute across one or more models. In the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, Fusion Max scored within two points of Opus 5.5 Max at half the cost and 40% less time per task. Copilot projects: Give Copilot a goal Available natively in the GitHub Copilot app starting today, Copilot projects let you run agent work across multiple repos in fully managed, parallel sessions. You have one place to track progress, make decisions, and direct what happens next. That means you can spend less time managing execution and more time deciding what’s worth building. Session continuity: Keep working across surfaces Your work shouldn’t restart when you switch devices or tools. Session continuity lets you start and follow the same cloud agent session across the GitHub app, VS Code, the CLI, and the web. Start from your phone at standup, steer it from VS Code at your desk, and check in on it from github.com at lunch. The agent keeps working in the cloud. Our multi-model harness that enables it is powerful, fast, and cost-efficient. Copilot automations: Learning from the results Copilot automations let you create AI-powered workflows within your repo. They run in the cloud, and you can kick them off manually or set them up to respond to an event or run on a schedule. That lets you coordinate agents to handle tasks such as issue triage and code review. And now, automations can learn…

articles.title: Octoverse: Commits, pushes, reach new highs in 2026 as developers build with agents
articles.content: Developers pushed code to GitHub 17.9 billion times in the past 12 months, more than in 2024 and 2025 combined. Behind that number are developers building what interests them and what their communities need. In Nepal, one developer built a flood bulletin on GitHub Pages with verified information on roads, rescue, weather, and power. It has since grown into Gati , a Nepali-first relay of official disaster alerts that runs on GitHub Pages and Actions. Elsewhere, developers at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory are creating software designed to run programs aboard spacecraft , and fans built open-source firmware that lets people customize their e-readers . Curiosity, aimed in every direction, at a scale GitHub hasn’t seen before. That growth happened quickly. Partway through the year, activity on GitHub bent sharply upward, just as agents went from something developers were trying out to something they were working alongside. Developers picked from more models than ever and built in industries we are highlighting in this report for the first time, from health care to agriculture. Octoverse is our chance to step back and look at the whole picture. This year, that picture is bigger than ever. Here is what stood out most: More AI, more of everything. Among repositories created this year, the average repo with an agent configuration file logged eight times as many commits as the average new repo without one. As of September, developers start more than 40% of pull requests with an agent. In March, it was 17%. For a growing share of work, the first move is now directing an agent, and review is how developers shape what comes back. Developers move fast on model choice. In September, 61% of GitHub Copilot users used more than one model, and requests spread across general purpose, deep reasoning and planning, and fast and lightweight models Builders are showing up from every field. This year, for the first time, we’re sharing our view of public repositories by industry. Repos serving mining, construction, health care, and agriculture have each grown several times over since 2022. Underneath it all, AI models and the harnesses built around them have advanced over the past year, and developers have more to choose from. Growth is moving quickly: one year into last year’s five-year developer growth projections, every country we projected has already closed at least a fifth of its distance to 2030, and our own forecasting models no longer agree on where it will go next. The year developers set a new pace This year was all about momentum. Developers pushed code changes to GitHub 17.9 billion times in the past 12 months, more than 2024 and 2025 combined. Commits across all repo types (public and private) climbed even faster to 34.3 billion, more than three times where they stood two years ago. Merged pull requests more than tripled to 1.3 billion over the same period, an average of 3.5 million a day. Agents were one of the tools developers leaned on hardest this year, pulling them deeper into daily work. Among repos created this year, the average repo with an agent configuration file logged eight times as many commits as the average new repo without one, sign that individuals and teams building with agents from day one are moving at a markedly different pace. Developers also relied on automations to keep projects moving. GitHub Actions ran a job 1,440 times every second this year. This equals 124 million times a day and is more than three times last year’s total. Developers merged more than 30 million Dependabot pull requests to keep dependencies current and reduce the use of known vulnerabilities, about double 2025’s pace. Our telemetry shows activity climbing steadily from January, then surging around June, as if developers everywhere saw new possibilities at once. Right around then, a cluster of industry-wide shifts landed: better underlying models, the harnesses and tools built around them, and the agents…

articles.title: FCC Approves Amazon Leo's $11.5 Billion Acquisition of Globalstar
articles.content: The FCC has approved (PDF) Amazon Leo's $11.5 billion acquisition of satellite operator Globalstar, giving the Starlink rival additional infrastructure and spectrum to expand into direct-to-device satellite connectivity. Engadget reports: You may not know Globalstar but have possibly used its services, as the company provides Apple's emergency satellite connectivity for compatible iPhones and Watches. Interestingly, Apple also held a 20 percent stake in Globalstar prior to its takeover. As part of the deal, Leo will power satellite services for supported iPhone and Apple Watch models. Leo, a rival to SpaceX's Starlink, has been active of late. The company recently announced that it has 400 satellites in orbit and revealed last month that it had launched high-quality satellite internet service in Uzbekistan. It's teaming up with Delta to eventually bring satellite internet to flights, as well. Amazon recently added six new Arianespace launches and aims to have more than 3,000 low-earth orbit satellites up in the near future, still well short of SpaceX's 11,000 satellites. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: 3 Questions: Why infrastructure is entering a defining era
articles.content: For centuries, infrastructure has evolved alongside technology. New materials and engineering techniques enabled taller buildings, longer bridges, and larger cities. Computing and digital technologies later transformed how infrastructure was designed, monitored, and operated. Now, the pace of change is accelerating, and challenges are arriving simultaneously. Climate change is increasing pressure on water, energy, and other resources. Artificial intelligence is beginning to transform engineering and design, and its energy needs, along with aging grid infrastructure, is creating significant challenges, as well as new opportunities. In addition, geopolitical complexity is exposing vulnerabilities in global supply chains, and demand for infrastructure is rising, particularly in the developing world. The result is a fundamental challenge: How can the world build the infrastructure it needs without simply repeating the extractive, carbon- and resource-intensive model of the 20th century? In this interview, Ali Jadbabaie, JR East Professor and head of the MIT Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, says the answer will require rethinking not only how infrastructure is designed and built, but how it is financed and operated, and bringing together the many stakeholders who shape those decisions. On Oct. 28, Jadbabaie will join experts from around the world in Madrid to explore these topics at the World Infrastructure Forum , which was co-founded by MIT’s Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, UPM, the World Bank Group, and the University of Texas at Austin. Q: Infrastructure has always evolved in response to technological advances. What makes this era different? A: In the 18th century, civil engineering emerged as the civilian counterpart to military engineering, building the dams, bridges, and canals of its time. Industrialization in the 19th century brought railways and sewage systems. In the early 20th century, the focus scaled up to buildings, highways, tunnels, and metro systems, and by mid-century the infrastructure needed to support megacities and skyscrapers. Every time technology has changed, with information technologies, computing, sensing, and, more recently, digital transformation, it has changed the shape of infrastructure. It has even changed the definition of what infrastructure is. Today, we consider the power grid, semiconductor manufacturing plants, and data centers part of infrastructure, along with wireless infrastructure like cellphone towers and the infrastructure for high-speed internet, just as much a part of our critical infrastructure as roads, water systems, and power grids. What is different now is the combination and speed of the changes we're facing. Climate change, resource constraints, and geopolitical instability are putting pressure on the way we designed infrastructure in the 20th century. At the same time, many people are moving out of poverty because of recent economic growth in the developing world. In fact, according to models, by 2028, for the first time in the history of humanity, the median human inhabitant of the planet will live off $10 a day. As more people move out of abject poverty, there will also be an increase in the demand for infrastructure. If we try to meet that demand using the same resource-intensive model we used in the 20th century, we simply won't have the resources to do it. The question then becomes: How do we use the remaining resources more efficiently? We need to find a way to provide more infrastructure while using less water, energy, and materials, and produce less carbon. This is where digital transformation and AI become potentially transformative. Faster and cheaper sensing, greater access to data, and better sensing, actuation, and control can help us make infrastructure decisions more efficiently. AI is slowly permeating the physical world, and we expect it to revolutionize the engineering design process, allowing us to explore many more…

articles.title: Serial ransomware crook gets 70 months behind bars for Nefilim, Hive roles
articles.content: Ukrainian ransomware crook Artem Stryzhak has been sentenced to 70 months in the slammer by a New York federal court for his role as an affiliate of the Nefilim and Hive ransomware gangs. Prosecutors believe the cybercriminal began working with Nefilim in or around June 2021, while living in Barcelona, Spain. The Nefilim ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation was known for targeting wealthy companies, with its operators encouraging affiliates to pursue businesses capable of paying substantial ransom demands. One of Nefilim's most high-profile attacks was on Australian logistics giant Toll Group in 2020, encrypting its files roughly three months after it suffered a separate Mailto ransomware attack. Court documents [PDF] state that Stryzhak agreed with alleged Nefilim boss Volodymyr Tymoshchuk , who remains at large, to pay the ransomware crew a 20 percent cut of the ransom proceeds he collected. Tymoshchuk told Stryzhak that his preference was for attacks to target companies based in the US, Canada, and Australia that turn over more than $100 million annually. This guidance was soon tweaked to encourage targeting companies in the same regions with more than $200 million in annual revenue. Prosecutors claim that around the time Stryzhak joined forces with Nefilim, he also signed up to the Hive ransomware operation as "one of its earliest affiliates," and used its platform to attack approximately seven victims. Hive's operators claimed they targeted circa 1,500 victims worldwide between June 2021 and January 2023. According to separate court documents [PDF], Hive's victims included a law firm and an Ohio hospital, which paid approximately $1.7 million in Bitcoin after the gang initially demanded $2 million during the COVID-19 pandemic. Before its infrastructure was seized in an international law enforcement operation in January 2023, Hive was known for attacking healthcare facilities during the COVID-19 pandemic, as well as being one of the ransomware groups that battered Costa Rica in 2022 . Brett Leatherman, assistant director at the FBI’s cyber branch, described Stryzhak as a “prolific cybercriminal” who played a role in groups that were responsible for more than $100 million in victim damages. “Today’s sentence reflects the seriousness of Stryzhak’s crimes and demonstrates the FBI’s global reach and extensive network of international partners,” he said. “Multiple field offices contributed to this investigation, and our work does not end here. We will continue to leverage every tool at our disposal to track down Stryzhak’s co-conspirators and hold them accountable, including Volodymyr Viktorovych Tymoshchuk.” Stryzhak was arrested by Spanish police in June 2024 before being extradited to the US in April 2025. In announcing Stryzhak's sentencing, the Justice Department took the opportunity to remind the public that rewards totaling up to $11 million are available for qualifying information about alleged Nefilim operator Volodymyr Tymoshchuk and other key ransomware suspects. ®

articles.title: Nvidia's open Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe combines transcription, translation, and speaker recognition
articles.content: Nvidia has released Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe, an open speech recognition model that handles transcription, speaker recognition, and translation and takes its instructions as text prompts. It leads several benchmarks and uses only a sixth of the active parameters of its strongest open rival. Nvidia is also shipping a dataset with more than 800,000 hours of speech, along with tools for fine-tuning. The article Nvidia's open Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe combines transcription, translation, and speaker recognition appeared first on The Decoder .

articles.title: Google and Apple hit with a combined fine of $47.6 million by South Korea’s watchdog
articles.content: South Korea on Wednesday fined Alphabet’s Google and Apple a combined 63.7 billion won ($47.6 million), saying they abused their dominance in app store markets by forcing local developers onto their own payment systems and by unfairly delaying app reviews. The Korea Media and Communications Commission, the country’s media and telecommunications regulator, spent years investigating the U.S. tech giants for allegedly violating a 2021 law that prohibits app store operators from forcing developers to use specific payment systems. The commission fined Google 42.9 billion won ($32 million) and Apple 20.8 billion won ($15.5 million) and ordered both companies to let South Korean developers use external payment links within their apps and to improve their app review procedures. Google and Apple did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The commission said Google and Apple unfairly pushed app developers toward their own in-app payment systems while barring payments through external websites. Although the companies technically allowed third-party payment systems within apps, they charged developers a 26% commission and withheld some features available through their own systems, effectively forcing developers to use only their in-app payment systems, the commission said. The commission said it also found instances where the companies delayed app reviews without clearly explaining to developers the reasons for the delays or when reviews would resume. It also accused Apple of charging South Korean developers higher commissions than developers elsewhere from 2015 to January 2023. South Korea has for years closely scrutinized the business practices of foreign technology companies operating in its market. In 2021, it became the first country to enforce a law prohibiting app market operators such as Google and Apple from requiring users to use their own in-app payment systems. —Kim Tong-Hyung, Associated Press

articles.title: Blue Origin leases former Bartell Drugs warehouse south of Seattle for new manufacturing site
articles.content: The Prologis Park SeaTac 3 industrial building in Des Moines, Wash. (Prologis Photo) Blue Origin is taking over an industrial building in Des Moines, Wash., where the Jeff Bezos-founded space company plans a mix of lab, development and light production work, the company confirmed to GeekWire. The 265,922-square-foot facility, known as Prologis Park SeaTac 3 , was previously a Bartell Drugs distribution center just south of Seattle-Tacoma International Airport. Blue Origin said that at full capacity over the long term, the site is expected to support hundreds of employees. KING 5 first reported the news Tuesday, citing a state environmental application filed in September that lists Blue Origin Manufacturing LLC at the building’s address, 21202 24th Ave. S. A pre-application under review by the city indicates the property could be used for research and development of commercial satellites, the station reported. Commercial real estate firm Newmark announced a lease for the entire building last week without naming the tenant. “The manufacturing project that will be using this property is cutting-edge and we are excited about the job growth and possibilities that it represents for our region,” Newmark Executive Vice Chairman Thad Mallory said in a news release . With roughly 33,000 residents, the small city of Des Moines is becoming something of an aerospace hub. Blue Origin’s new location is around the corner from where Shield AI is building X-Forge 3, a 420,000-square-foot facility that will make the company’s X-BAT autonomous fighter jet. Shield AI said last month it expects to have 4,000 workers in the region by the early 2030s, and that it’s looking for another 1 million square feet. “It’s all about labor and access to power,” Mallory told KING 5, referring to the advanced manufacturing projects coming to the area. Blue Origin is headquartered in nearby Kent, Wash., about 5 miles from the Des Moines site. The company is working to get its New Glenn rocket flying again after one exploded during a ground engine test in May, which damaged its Florida launch pad. New Glenn is slated to carry Blue’s Blue Moon Mark 2 lander on NASA’s Artemis 3 mission, a test in Earth orbit planned for mid-2027 ahead of a crewed moon landing targeted for 2028.
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser

articles.title: AI component hikes force the world's largest PC makers to return manufacturing capacity to China
articles.content: HP, Asus, and Acer have reportedly moved some of their manufacturing capacity back into China as increasing component costs — driven by AI — bite into their margins. According to Nikkei Asia , increasing bill-of-materials costs have made China’s experienced workforce, relatively lower prices, and established supply chain ecosystem a more attractive option. However, they are not going back to traditional suppliers like Foxconn, who have focused their production capacity on AI data centers. Instead, they’re signing contracts with smaller Chinese contract manufacturers, like Luxshare, Huaqin Technology, and Longcheer Technology, that are trying to establish themselves in PC manufacturing. Go deeper with TH Premium: AI and data centers (Image credit: Microsoft) The data center cooling state of play The custom AI ASIC state of play America’s AI chip rules keep changing — and the rest of the world is paying the price GTC 2026: Ian Buck press Q&A transcript — VP of Hyperscale and HPC speaks out on shelving CPX and shipping LPU decode this year Demand for data center CPUs has surged, and AI agents are responsible Many PC brands slowly moved out of China in 2024 and 2025 as the U.S.’s sanctions and tariffs on China have increased prices and forced them to find friendlier nations. While these nations do not have established supply chains and expertise like China, it at least spreads the risk as manufacturers avoid getting caught up in geopolitical tensions. However, it seems that rising component prices have forced them to move back some of their capacity into China. The biggest culprit is the AI-induced memory and storage chip shortage, which has caused memory prices to climb an unprecedented 500% in 12 months. More than that, other parts like PCBs and fiberglass cloth used in motherboard manufacturing are seeing increasing prices, which Acer chairperson and CEO Jason Chen bemoaned as suppliers hyping shortage fears to protect margins. While tech companies aren’t abandoning their “China+1” diversification strategy, the mature industry in China is helping offset increased component costs. Aside from that, the Chinese contract manufacturers often have better access to memory chips from domestic manufacturers like CXMT. "These Chinese contract manufacturers have been telling potential clients and computer makers that working with them could be a good option for securing better access to Chinese-made memory chips," a supply chain manager in the computer ecosystem told Nikkei Asia . "They are marketing themselves as a good alternative to even help sort out the supply chain." Moving back some manufacturing capacity into China is easing some of PC manufacturers’ cost concerns, but it’s also negatively impacting the newly established supply chains in Southeast Asia. "We built two new production lines in Thailand for the PC clients, and now they are moving substantial orders back to China,” one manager at a PC component supplier told the publication. “Those two lines have not yet turned profitable, and I don't know when they will add the orders back." Unfortunately, building an entire supply chain for PC manufacturing is slow and expensive. The U.S. has been trying to accomplish this for years, and, so far, only Anduril has attempted to build laptops with 90% of its component costs coming from the U.S. and other allied countries . Even then, it expects its devices to be around 20% more expensive than the competition, which it could afford by offering them mostly to critical industries that demand supply chain security, like the government and the military. But if you’re a PC manufacturer vying for customers in the consumer market, you’re likely incentivized to find the lowest possible costs to be able to compete in pricing.
articles.author: Jowi Morales

articles.title: Amazon tells engineers to stop ‘tokenmaxxing’ to look productive
articles.content: Amazon wants its engineers to quit chasing token counts, warning that heavy AI usage does not automatically mean better work. In updated engineering guidelines published on October 27, the company laid out how developers and managers should gauge AI’s real impact — and the takeaway is blunt: consuming more tokens is not the same as delivering more value. Amazon is not backing away from the technology, though. “We are certain that whatever future best practices are, AI will be at the center of software engineering practice,” the company wrote. Go deeper with TH Premium: AI and data centers (Image credit: Microsoft) The data center cooling state of play The custom AI ASIC state of play America’s AI chip rules keep changing — and the rest of the world is paying the price GTC 2026: Ian Buck press Q&A transcript — VP of Hyperscale and HPC speaks out on shelving CPX and shipping LPU decode this year Demand for data center CPUs has surged, and AI agents are responsible The guidance targets ‘ tokenmaxxing ,’ a practice where employees deliberately inflate their AI usage to look productive on internal dashboards. According to the memo, metrics such as AI adoption rates, token consumption, code changes, and code reviews become ‘deeply flawed’ when they are disconnected from actual results. Turning them into targets, Amazon says, encourages wasteful behavior that clashes with its emphasis on ‘frugality and simplicity’ and can raise both compute bills and software complexity. The company’s preferred yardstick is long-term results. “We believe that it is best to measure, and be measured by, long-term outcomes,” Amazon wrote. That does not mean managers should ignore usage data altogether, as input metrics remain useful when examined ‘with care and judgment’ alongside other indicators. Amazon suggests looking at both the teams using AI the least and those using it the most to determine whether adoption is translating into better delivery. The push comes as Amazon, under CEO Andy Jassy, has been weaving AI deeply into its sprawling operations. Jassy said earlier this year that the technology will ‘change the scope and speed’ of everyday work, and he has suggested that automation could shrink the company’s corporate workforce over the next few years — though he also expects it to create ‘other jobs.’ The memo also pushes back on the idea that every task needs an AI tool. If current tooling does not benefit someone’s work, Amazon says, that is ‘a finding, not a failing.’ Engineers who can explain where today’s tools fall short are demonstrating judgment rather than reluctance to adopt AI. In May, it emerged that Amazon employees were using AI unnecessarily to boost internal usage scores, amid pressure to use the company's tools. Workers reportedly used MeshClaw , an internal AI agent capable of handling tasks such as deploying code and interacting with Slack, to inflate their token counts. Notably, Amazon is not the only company rethinking how it spends on AI. Uber president and COO Andrew Macdonald said in May that higher token usage has yet to translate into useful consumer features. “That link is not there yet,” he said . The remark stands out because Uber’s CTO previously revealed that the company had burned through its entire 2026 Claude Code budget by April. Accenture appears to also be wrestling with the same problem on behalf of its clients. Leaked audio obtained by 404 Media in June captures executives acknowledging that token spending is climbing fast as companies move from simple chatbots to agentic workflows, and that nobody can reliably predict what a given task will cost or whether it was worth the money. Accenture’s agentic AI strategy lead described it as ‘not a niche problem,’ and the firm is reportedly building an advisory tool called ‘Token IQ’ to help customers manage the bill. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has previously acknowledged that AI token costs had become 'a huge issue ', as companies faced mounting bills from heavy AI…

articles.title: How Google fumbled the frontend with Angular 2
articles.content: A cartoon from an ex-Google software engineer, titled “Welcome to Google,” made the rounds a while back. It featured two diverging roads, neither passable. One was the main road, marked as deprecated (“don’t even think about it,” the sign read). The new road, however, was marked as still under construction (“Danger”), and so was unusable as well. That was the no-win choice two million frontend developers faced in 2014, when Google unexpectedly deprecated its popular JavaScript framework, AngularJS, in favor of Angular 2, which had a radically different architecture, a confusing name, no upgrade path, and wasn’t even fully released yet. So, many developers turned the wheel and headed to Reactville or Vuetown instead. How Google botched the Angular upgrade provides timely lessons in how not to update a software package, which former Google Developer Advocate Stephen Fluin outlined in a talk at the All Things Open conference last week. “Uncertainty kills motivation,” said Fluin. “When you're taking away everything [developers] know and love, they're going to feel disheartened.” Fluin is now head of developer relations for Buildkite , but he worked for Google from 2016 to 2021 on the Angular project. “Things were a little bit rough at the time. It was a bit of a death march,” he told the audience. “We had no idea when Angular 2 was going to come out, and the core fundamentals of Angular kept changing.” From AngularJS to Angular 2 Google had good reasons for updating Angular. The AngularJS team had been snatched from Google’s infrastructure division and placed under its ad division, where the software could be more fully exploited. To support operations of that size, Angular needed greater rigor. The original AngularJS was launched in 2009 as a side project of Google engineer Miško Hevery , who wanted to extend HTML. Google pulled AngularJS into an internal project because Google developers found it easier to work with than the Java-based Google Web Toolkit ( GWT ). The framework quickly caught on with outside web developers too, who readily understood the angle brackets of HTML (hence the name) and wanted more interactive components. Hevery built AngularJS 1.3 with a traditional controller model, which handled all user input, logic and data transport under the JavaScript $scope object. Angular 2, announced at the ng-europe 2014 conference, was a major shift in architecture. It shifted to a component model, with each HTML template enjoying its own class properties. After a forced, unhappy dalliance with Google's Dart , the team rewrote Angular completely in TypeScript, with no backward compatibility whatsoever. It was a lot to take in, and the introductory talk at ng-europe seemed to spook Angular developers more than inspire them. For each discarded feature, the speakers displayed a graphic of a tombstone (“RIP Controllers”) and played a recording of a church bell tolling in the background. “That talk is still infamous today for what it did to the community,” Fluin said. “All these things that you know and love about AngularJS are gone. They're dead. And nobody knew this was coming.” In general, it was not a good time for software migrations, Fluin noted in his talk. Python was having a rough time migrating from version 2 to 3 , as was the KDE desktop moving from version 4 to version 5. And the rocky transition from GNOME 2 to 3 still loomed in the rearview mirror for many. What's in a name? “If you're trying to bring your developers with you, give them a path. Don't just kill your old thing and then not have a new thing ready,” Fluin advised. Many devs defected to React and Vue.js , two other JavaScript frontend frameworks that also embraced the component model and were already in production. In the 2016 State of JS Survey , React was the most popular frontend framework, with 53 percent of JS devs reporting that they had used it. Angular’s audience was heavily bifurcated; 30 percent still used the classic version while only 13…

articles.title: Amazon earnings preview: AWS is booked up, and Wall Street wants to know what comes next
articles.content: Andy Jassy says Amazon “could invest a lot more” in AI infrastructure “and it wouldn’t be a bad use of capital.” (GeekWire File Photo / Todd Bishop) Amazon reports third-quarter earnings Thursday afternoon with more demand for its cloud services than it can serve, driven by AI labs such as Anthropic and OpenAI along with growth in its traditional cloud business. One big question for Wall Street going into the report is what Amazon might signal about next year’s spending as it tries to keep up with that demand. CEO Andy Jassy said on an Andreessen Horowitz podcast last week that AWS capacity is largely booked for this year and next, along with “a good chunk of ’28.” Amazon has said it expects to spend about $220 billion on capital expenditures this year, largely on AI and cloud infrastructure, up from its earlier plan of $200 billion. Even at that level, Jassy said, Amazon is “leaving a meaningful amount of demand on the table.” Past spending pushed Amazon’s free cash flow to negative $7.6 billion for the 12 months ending in June, as the cost to add data centers, chips and other equipment exceeded the cash its operations brought in. Jassy gave no indication of slowing down, saying the company “could invest a lot more and it wouldn’t be a bad use of capital.” Core numbers: Analysts expect revenue of about $202 billion, up 12% from a year ago, according to Yahoo Finance. That’s at the top of Amazon’s own forecast of $197 billion to $202 billion. Analysts expect earnings of $1.96 per share, about the same as a year ago. Amazon’s sales growth will likely look slower this time, about 12%, down from 20% last quarter. A big reason is timing. Prime Day, the company’s biggest sales event of the year, fell in the second quarter this year, rather than the third quarter as it did last year, so this quarter is up against a tougher comparison. Amazon estimated in July that the shift would take nearly 4 percentage points off its growth rate this quarter. It hits online store sales hardest: analysts expect them to grow only about 3%, according to Zacks. AWS: Amazon Web Services, the company’s cloud business, generates the majority of its operating profit. AWS revenue grew 37% to $42.2 billion in the second quarter, its fastest pace since 2021 and the fifth straight quarter of faster growth. Analysts expect AWS revenue of about $45.4 billion this time, up 37.5%, according to Zacks. Wedbush is more optimistic, projecting growth of about 41%. AWS had $496 billion in signed contracts it hadn’t yet delivered as of June, more than double the year before. That means its growth depends largely on how quickly Amazon can bring new data centers online. “Capacity, not demand, is the constraint,” Yorkville Ives analyst Dan Ives wrote of the industry in a note Sunday. Jassy said on the a16z podcast that running AI models is still “an order of magnitude too expensive” for businesses to use them widely, and that Amazon’s custom chips, including its Trainium AI processors, are a big piece of bringing that cost down. Amazon said in July that its chip business was on pace for more than $25 billion in annual revenue. Anthropic stake: Amazon’s reported earnings could look very different. That’s because its profit fluctuates significantly depending on the value of its stake in Anthropic. Last quarter, $53.4 billion in pre-tax gains, mostly on Anthropic, pushed Amazon’s earnings to $5.75 per share, against expectations of $1.82. Anthropic filed paperwork Monday for a planned IPO on the Nasdaq. Amazon’s stake in the AI company was valued at about $190 billion as of June 30, according to Amazon’s latest quarterly filing. That includes about $92 billion in gains on convertible notes, a form of loan that turns into stock, which haven’t yet been counted in Amazon’s profit. Those notes would convert to…

articles.title: FCC rebuffs TP-Link again as it attempts to sell Wi-Fi 8 gear in the US
articles.content: TP-Link has been trying everything in its power to gain conditional approval from the Federal Communications Commission (FCC). According to a new Bloomberg report , the FCC is citing discrepancies in power levels in TP-Link routers as the latest roadblock on its path to selling new Wi-Fi 8 products stateside . In letters dated October 15, 2026, the FCC Office of Engineering and Technology made some damning claims about TP-Link's reporting practices. Specifically, the FCC alleged that TP-Link "included false or incorrect information in its applications” related to equipment authorizations for four individual router models (including high-end Archer models ). For a company that truly needs to dot every "i" and cross every "t" when it comes to a Trump administration that is increasingly skeptical of TP-Link's past ties and motives, any perceived missteps are even more magnified. However, in addition to the alleged wonky product information provided to the FCC, perhaps more troubling is that three of the four routers under scrutiny also had higher-than-allowed power usage levels. In addition to power limits, the FCC's testing regimen for routers includes evaluations of electromagnetic compatibility (EMC), radio frequency (RF) emissions, and national security compliance . The latter has been a big sticking point with the FCC and the U.S. Department of Defense given the proliferation of TP-Link networking gear in civilian and governmental capacities. We reached out to TP-Link about the FCC’s findings and were provided with the following statement: "Routine spot checks have been a standard FCC practice across the consumer electronics industry for many years, and individual product test results can occasionally vary. TP-Link Systems fully supports the FCC’s Office of Engineering and Technology and its role of ensuring that all manufacturers adhere to prescribed specifications for their certified products. We remain fully committed to working collaboratively with the FCC to resolve any technical questions that arise — and if necessary, address any confirmed technical issues as swiftly as possible." It will likely take a lot more convincing to appease the FCC, which has so far given TP-Link the cold shoulder. And it’s not just the FCC; members of Congress and multiple state attorneys general have filed their grievances with TP-Link over alleged consumer privacy violations and Chinese ties. For its part, TP-Link has made some significant moves to get in the good graces of the U.S. government, even while competitors like Amazon , Asus , and Netgear have sailed through compliance checks to gain conditional approval to sell wireless products in the U.S. Besides moving its U.S. headquarters to California, the company earlier this month announced a $1 billion joint venture with Key Tronic to manufacture Wi-Fi 8 routers in the U.S.
