articles.title: Thin, Light and Built for Everything: NVIDIA RTX Spark Windows Laptops Gain New Models, Agent Tools and Games
articles.content: NVIDIA RTX Spark powers thin and light laptops built for everything that developers, creators and gamers do. RTX Spark laptops are now available from ASUS, Dell, HP, Lenovo, Microsoft and MSI. These powerful systems combine an NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPU and an NVIDIA Grace CPU in a single superchip with up to 128GB of unified memory and up to 1 petaflop of FP4 AI performance. That puts the NVIDIA CUDA platform, RTX graphics and the capabilities of a personal AI supercomputer inside premium Windows laptops built to go anywhere. New and expected RTX Spark updates, coming soon, include: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe, an open weight speech model for transcription, speaker attribution and translation is available on RTX Spark. The LFM3 family of open models with day-zero support. Resource management controls in NVIDIA App to allocate GPU resources between foreground apps and background agents. Phantom Blade Zero , S-GAME’s highly-anticipated action role-playing game, launches with ray tracing and NVIDIA DLSS 4.5. Experience Minecraft with path tracing and DLSS with RTX Remix1.6, available now for RTX Spark. Turn Recorded Audio Into Useful Information With NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe Introduced today, NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe is a new, open weight speech model that turns recorded conversations into useful information. Instead of needing multiple models for transcription, speaker labels and translation, developers can use one promptable model that handles all three, plus questions about the audio. It transcribes 40 languages, including seven Indic languages. Developers guide the model with plain-language prompts. For example, for a single recorded meeting, users can ask it to: “Transcribe this recording and label each speaker.” “Translate this audio into English.” “List what decisions were made in this meeting.” Prompts can also include product terms and formatting conventions, which helps the model handle specialized vocabulary in fields like healthcare, financial services and customer service. Because the weights are open, developers can choose where audio is processed, from a desktop to the cloud. Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe ranks No. 1 on the Hugging Face Open ASR and No. 2 among open weight models on Artificial Analysis — delivering leading accuracy with approximately 4.3 billion active parameters, 80% fewer than the No. 1 open weight model, making high-quality, intelligent transcription more practical on local hardware. It’s available today on Hugging Face . Quantized versions are coming soon, so developers can run Transcribe locally onNVIDIA RTX Spark and DGX Spark systems, Jetson AGX Thor devices or scale up on NVIDIA Blackwell data center GPUs. NVFP4 versions will be deployable through NeMo-Speech.cpp or vLLM. Learn more in the NVIDIA technical blog . Control How Agents and PC Apps Share GPU Resources On RTX Spark, users can have long-running agents working alongside their favorite applications. Both share the system’s GPU compute, and the right balance of resources depends on what matters to users at that moment. With the new resource management feature in NVIDIA App , users can now choose how GPU resources are shared. They can prioritize their foreground app for the best performance, or give their background-running agent more resources to get work done faster. Access control resource sharing from System > Advanced in the NVIDIA App. This feature requires hardware-accelerated GPU scheduling to be enabled in Windows Settings. Liquid AI : One Model Family, Many Ways to Work Liquid AI’s LFM3 provides a new generation of Liquid Foundation Models designed for specialized tasks. The family spans text, vision, audio, omni and decision models built on one shared backbone, with base and post-trained models available as open weights. The models are compact and fast: Liquid AI’s new 1.7-billion-parameter base model outperforms its previous 2.6-billion-parameter base model. These models support local workflows such as agents…

articles.title: Nvidia launches a promptable transcription model
articles.content: Nvidia on Wednesday launched Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe, its latest multilingual transcription model. The new open-weight model, the company says, ranks first on Hugging Face’s Open ASR open model leaderboard for English, with an average word error rate of 5.33%, and also sits at the top of two speaker-attribution benchmarks. But what’s maybe even more interesting is that this is a promptable transcription model. Being promptable here means that the user can give the model specific instructions before it listens. Typically, that means setting the context for the transcription by telling the model that a given audio file is a medical discussion in English, for example, and giving it a list of medical terms. Users can also tell the model to label each speaker or ask it questions about the audio. They can request a verbatim transcript or a cleaned-up version, and tell it how to format numbers, for example. Credit: Nvidia. Nvidia bundles these capabilities, along with translation, into a single checkpoint, which could simplify the work of building applications around them. Ideally, setting this context reduces the error rate. The trade-off is that these models are much larger than traditional transcription models, which are often under a billion parameters in size. Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe is a 30B mixture-of-experts model with 4 billion active parameters. This isn’t a completely new concept, though. We’ve recently seen some other promptable speech-to-text models like Mistral’s Voxtral models and AssemblyAI’s Universal 3 Pro . Nvidia, though, is able to rival Voxtral’s error rate with far fewer active parameters. On Artificial Analysis’s benchmark, Nemotron scores a 2.81% word error rate, compared with Voxtral Small’s 2.77%, while using about 4 billion active parameters versus 24 billion. That comparison measures accuracy against active parameter counts, though, rather than runtime or memory requirements. The model can transcribe 40 languages — and translate 31 of those to or from English. Speaker attribution works for 13 of those languages, and it can distinguish between up to eight speaker voices. Audio Q&A was trained in English. The model handles recordings up to an hour long. It’s built for recorded audio, though, and doesn’t support live streaming. Credit: Nvidia. Developers can serve the model with vLLM or run it locally with NeMo-Speech.cpp . Nvidia says it runs on a single GPU, with supported hardware ranging from Jetson AGX Thor and DGX Spark to Blackwell data-center GPUs. Since this is an open-weight model (under the OpenMDW-1.1 license), users can fine-tune it to their needs in order to reduce the error rate by using NeMo Speech’s fine-tuning tools, among other tools. In a medical transcription case study, Nvidia says fine-tuning reduced word error rate on held-out speakers from 22.44% with its best prompt to 12.17%, a 45.8% relative reduction. The complete adaptation workflow took about 14 GPU-hours on a single GB300. Nvidia is also releasing Granary v2, a reusable data curation pipeline built with NeMo Curator, along with public manifests covering roughly 463,062 hours across 48 languages and 16 source corpora. Developers can run the pipeline on their own recordings to prepare their data for customization. These figures describe the dataset release, not Transcribe’s full training mixture or its sampling weights. The post Nvidia launches a promptable transcription model appeared first on The New Stack .
articles.author: Frederic Lardinois

articles.title: Fake videos possibly linked to Russia are targeting these two Democratic Senate candidates
articles.content: Social media videos believed to be produced with artificial intelligence and linked to Russia are misusing real people’s names and photographs to spread disinformation about two Democratic Senate candidates in the final stretch of midterm voting . One of the targets is Sherrod Brown, who is running against Republican Sen. Jon Husted in Ohio. The video, which appears to include some AI manipulation , depicts a newscast and includes pictures of Haya Akbik, who interned for Brown several years ago, and other former staff members. It was appalling to Akbik, who told The Associated Press that any claims attributed to her in the clip are “completely made up.” “It’s my name, it’s my reputation, making this allegation, and it’s just completely false,” she said. “And it harms the senator, someone else, in the process. So, it’s just messed up.” The videos demonstrate how foreign adversaries continue to use a familiar playbook to try to influence American voters who are deciding which party controls Congress next year. The threat could be magnified with AI, a powerful tool for fabricating damaging information that can sometimes appear very real. Another target is James Talarico , who is running against Republican Ken Paxton for a Senate seat in Texas. The video, also believed to include some AI manipulation, is framed as a direct-to-camera confessional from a former student of Talarico. “The most powerful people in the world know they can’t beat James Talarico with the truth, so they’re slandering him with AI deepfakes, foreign bots, and conspiracy theories to protect their broken, corrupt political system,” Talarico spokesperson JT Ennis said in a statement. The social media company X has taken down the initial posts that shared the videos and suspended the users for violating the platform’s rules. However, copies could still be found online Tuesday — some with hundreds of shares — demonstrating how difficult it can be to contain disinformation that can proliferate in the final days of an election. Experts see a resemblance to Russian clips from 2024 The videos resemble clips from a Russian network known as Storm-1516 that targeted former Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris and her running mate, Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz, two years ago. The new ones bear similar hallmarks and are likely products of the same network, according to Clemson University professor and media forensics expert Darren Linvill. He found that the accounts that shared recent material had also shared former content from Storm-1516. The Russian Embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In the past, it has denied interfering in U.S. elections. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which has publicly identified some videos as Russian disinformation in past election cycles, also didn’t respond to a request for comment. Hany Farid, a Dartmouth College professor who studies artificial intelligence deepfakes, said his analyses showed that videos targeting Brown and Talarico were likely either generated or manipulated using the technology. He noted the video targeting Brown is a “fairly low-tech fake.” The other one, targeting Talarico, is likely generated by AI and “it is consistent with previous disinformation campaigns released close to Election Day,” Farid said. Akbik said the video featuring her shows the importance of Congress regulating “AI slop on the internet.” “This is so damaging,” she said. —Ali Swenson, Associated Press

articles.title: Microsoft faces potential vote: Shareholders curious about its plans to tackle emissions
articles.content: Trillium Asset Management wants Microsoft to explain how it will meet its 2030 greenhouse gas (GHG) emission targets, and is backing a shareholder proposal to request this information at the firm’s next shareholder meeting. The cloud and software biz set itself lofty environmental goals back in 2020 , aiming to be become "carbon-negative" by 2030, and to have removed the equivalent of all the carbon it has ever emitted by 2050. But since the start of the decade, an explosion in AI development and demand for ever more complex models has seen a boom in demand for high-performance compute infrastructure and a construction wave to deliver new datacenters to house it all in. Microsoft is one of the firms to profit from this huge demand, with its cloud division making $214.4 billion in revenue for the fiscal year 2026 ended June 30, a 27 percent year-on-year increase. This has also caused Microsoft’s emissions to head in the wrong direction, with figures from the company’s most recent Environmental Sustainability Report showing that these have increased from 13 million tons of CO 2 equivalent in 2020 to 20 million tons in 2025. However, Microsoft estimates that without the carbon reduction initiatives it has already put in place, emissions would now be much higher, somewhere near 34 million tons. The increase is largely accounted for by indirect emissions (Scope 3) from the construction and provisioning of datacenters to meet that demand for cloud services and AI training. But as The Register pointed out, 2025 saw a growing contribution from Scope 2, due to generation of energy the company purchased. This represents 13 percent of total emissions – up from 2 percent in 2024. Now Trillium Asset Management, financial advisors specializing in sustainable and responsible investing, is urging Microsoft shareholders to vote for Proposal 4 during their annual meeting scheduled for December 8. In an SEC filing , the proposal asks Microsoft to disclose additional information illustrating how it will manage climate commitments. This disclosure should go beyond existing disclosures, at reasonable cost, omitting proprietary information, and be made annually. The proposal notes that when Microsoft first announced its carbon negative goal, it said progress required "not just a bold goal but a detailed plan," and that transparency was one of the guiding principles for this climate plan. It states that emissions are now 62 percent above the 2020 baseline, and simply asks Microsoft to apply the principles it articulated in 2020; show the plan, be candid about the math, and explain how it will adapt. In the filing, Trillium warns that falling short of its climate targets may create risk to Microsoft’s credibility, which can influence investor trust. If Microsoft is in danger of failing to meet its 2030 commitments, it could suffer reputational harm, and the filing claims it is already the subject of legal action by investors alleging insufficient disclosure of its AI and cloud spending. On the flip side, it says that disclosure of a climate transition plan will likely prove valuable to large institutional investors who view climate change as a systemic risk to future economic growth. We asked Microsoft for comment, but it already recommended in another SEC filing that shareholders vote against the proposal, arguing it fails to show that Microsoft’s existing disclosures are insufficient for investors to assess its climate-related strategy and performance. Instead, the firm says that the proposal requests a collection of new disclosures that go beyond not just legal and regulatory requirements, but also established voluntary climate-reporting frameworks. The proposal seeks hypothetical scenarios, contingency plans and other forward-looking information that is inherently uncertain and subject to change, Microsoft states, saying it will remain focused on its Sustainability Report and other environmental reporting while meeting any new disclosure mandates…

articles.title: Otter adds ‘Work’ mode to automate more meeting-related tasks
articles.content: Otter has added a new Work mode to its AI Chat assistant, expanding the range of tasks it can carry out before and after meetings. It’s part of a wider drive by Otter — which received $320 million in funding last week — to move beyond meeting transcription and into automating tasks and workflows. The Work interface, announced Tuesday, is accessible in the AI Chat prompt box, alongside the Chat option. While Chat allows users to ask questions, generate content, and retrieve information, Work is aimed at multi-step actions, Otter said. It’s a similar approach to other AI assistants, such as Claude and ChatGPT, that separate simpler chat functionality from newer agentic capabilities. Prior to a meeting, Otter users can prompt Work to generate briefing documents based on information collated from previous calls and data from connected applications. After a meeting ends, the AI assistant can draft emails, generate documents — including Word and Notion docs, PDFs, and interactive web pages — and update Salesforce records. The AI assistant requires human approval before completing tasks, an Otter spokesperson said. The capabilities expand on functions already available with AI Chat’s existing Advanced mode. Otter will now remove the Express and Advanced options from the AI Chat interface. Work mode is available now to all paid Otter users. There are no usage limits, Otter said — this differs from the Chat mode, which allocates a certain number of queries each month depending on a customer’s payment plan. The feature updates reflect how meeting note taking is rapidly moving from data capture to workflow automation, said Irwin Lazar, principal analyst at Metrigy. “That is, vendors are delivering solutions that allow meeting notes to be actionable, based on context both from within meetings, as well as from other connected platforms,” he said. Lazar pointed to similar functionality emerging in other meeting systems such as Microsoft’s facilitator in Teams and Cisco’s Webex meeting agent. The vast majority (91%) of business users want meeting note-takers to access and act on context from outside a meeting, according to a global study of 403 organizations in Metrigy’s “Workplace Collaboration & Employee Experience: 2027” report. In addition to the Work mode, Otter announced that its Live Assist feature is now available to enterprise customers, and will expand access to all paid Otter accounts in the coming weeks. Live Assist, announced in April, provides private guidance to a user during a call, such as suggesting questions and tracking meeting “objectives.” “I see this kind of widget assist a lot in external-facing customer support roles, but for internal productivity meetings, this is quite unique,” said Thomas Randall, a research director at Infotech. However he said that Otter faces from other meeting software vendors which are also integrating AI capabilities into their platforms. “So I don’t see Otter becoming a center of work, though its new functionality will be of great assistance to pre-existing users,” said Randall. Related: Cisco brings collaborative agents and Claude into Webex chats AI notetakers at work could leave companies at risk for lawsuits

articles.title: Corsair Warthog case review: A rugged, military-themed chassis with plenty of airflow
articles.content: Fractal arguably kicked off the wood accent PC trend with the North line, and the company says its new Summit case is built for “...expressive, high-performance systems combining distinctive Scandinavian design and advanced cooling potential.” The chassis sports FSC-certified wood (timber verified to come from responsibly managed, socially beneficial, and economically viable forests) for details like the front surround and solid wood feet. There’s no doubt it’s a good-looking case, but if you want to show off the wood, you’ll want to stick to the Chalk White or Black versions, as it blends in with the Blackout SKU we tested. Corsair’s latest case, the Warthog, is a military-inspired chassis that resembles a fuel canister (jerry can) you’d see on military vehicles. Based loosely on the Vengeance C70 case from 2012, which looked more like an ammunition container, the new Warthog evolved into a much better-looking, more functional chassis for today’s hardware in either of the two colorways. The Warthog does resemble its predecessor, and Corsair borrowed some features from the C70 while updating the design with “...even more rugged exterior, significantly more expansion options, and an emphasis on excellent airflow throughout the chassis,” and the company largely succeeded. The Warthog updates include the InfiniRail Fan Mounting System for flexible fan mounting, a pegboard motherboard tray for custom cable management, room for today’s massive video cards (plus built-in GPU support), and three mounting locations for 360mm radiators and 13 120mm fans. It even has bump guards on the front I/O for that all-in military aesthetic. The fighter jet-style front IO includes USB ports, one fast USB 3.2 Gen2x2 (20 Gbps) Type-C port, plus an on/off button for a unique integrated light on the back of the case that illuminates the rear IO area and down. If you’re into the military look, the Corsair Warthog ($179) and Warthog RS ($199 with fans) absolutely nails it, with plenty of other features that make it a compelling mid-tower chassis. We'll cover more details inside and outside the chassis, showcasing the features and any issues we encounter during the build. We'll also run the case through thermal and noise testing to show how it performs compared to others and whether it could make our best PC cases list. Below are the case's specifications from Corsair. Corsair Warthog Product Specifications Type Mid-Tower Dimensions (H x L x W) 21.4 x 21 x 11.1-inches (546 x 534 x 284mm) Motherboard Support Mini-ITX, Micro ATX, ATX, E-ATX Back-connect Motherboard Support Yes Color Olive Drab Black Storage Support (1) 3.5-inch (2) 2.5-inch PCIe Expansion Slots 7 Fan Support Top - 3x120/2x140mm Front - 3x120/2x140/2x200mm Bottom - 3x120mm Side: 3x120/2x140mm Rear - 1x120/140mm Pre-installed fans (3) RS Series (120mm rear, 2x200mm front) Radiator Support Front - 360/280/240mm Top - 360/280/240mm Side - 360/280/240mm Rear - 140/120mm CPU Cooler Clearance 190mm GPU Clearance 393mm (w/ front fans) 405mm (w/o front fans) Vertical GPU Support Yes (requires riser card) PSU Length 200mm Dust Filters Front, Bottom, and Side Other features 3x pre-installed fans, integrated GPU support, Infinrail system, light on rear I/O, Military theme MSRP $179.99 (w/o fans) $199.99 (w/pre-installed fans) Warranty 2 Years Features of the Warthog ▶️ External Features Externally, the Warthog doesn’t look like many other cases. Sure, it has the general shape of a classic mid-tower, but the front and windowed panel break up the monotony we’re used to, with bars resembling a fuel tank breaking up the window pane and front of the chassis. The front and side panels also use Corsair’s steel 3D-Y perforations (also found on the 4000) for increased airflow, and they look different from most other cases. It also has a military-inspired front I/O, sturdy built-in steel handles, and the familiar army olive drab color (it also comes in black). It just screams military industrial design. Future…

articles.title: What happens when the agent is long gone, but its access key lives on?
articles.content: Imagine: There’s a line on the credential report that no one on the platform team can explain. An IAM user called research-agent-2 has an access key created 14 months ago that was last used 11 months ago. And it’s still active. The project it supported closed long ago, and the person who approved it doesn’t even work at the company anymore. While this example is hypothetical, the lifecycle problem isn’t. This doesn’t require carelessness. An agent is created for a task, the task ends, and nobody revisits its access. A departing person triggers offboarding; a finished agent just leaves a closed tab. AWS IAM user access keys don’t expire automatically, so a forgotten key stays valid until somebody disables or deletes it. “A departing person triggers offboarding; a finished agent just leaves a closed tab.” OWASP puts improper offboarding first in its 2025 Top 10 for non-human identities , and the remedy reads like this series’ premise: retire what’s no longer needed, and give the rest an accountable owner. The hard part is knowing what exists. The problem is that attackers move faster than an annual audit ever could. In September 2026, GreyNoise documented an AI-orchestrated campaign against PaperCut servers: the attacker went from an empty workspace to remote code execution at a real victim in under four hours, and once launched, the campaign compromised at least eleven organizations in 26 seconds. That wasn’t an attack using abandoned AWS IAM keys. It shows how quickly exposed access becomes useful once an attacker is in, and why slow inventory and revocation are dangerous. An agent’s access can outlive its purpose unless someone governs its lifecycle. The last three articles covered attaching an owner at discovery , reassigning one before a last day , and what happens when the owner is an agent . Credentials add a related problem, with one distinction. An agent’s deployment identity is what authenticates it, or the deployment platform, to a cloud account. “A forgotten VM costs money; a forgotten credential can grant access.” A provisioned credential is a persistent key, secret, or token that a deployment creates for some other workload; the two have different owners and revocation procedures. A forgotten VM costs money; a forgotten credential can grant access. The remedy is still a query, a policy, and a clock, each used for the part of the problem it can solve. 1. The query that finds keys no one is using CloudQuery can sync AWS IAM credential reports into aws_iam_credential_reports when that table is enabled in the source configuration. The report lists up to two access-key slots per user. This query, written for the ClickHouse dialect CloudQuery Platform uses, takes the latest synced row for each report, turns the slots into rows, and returns active IAM user keys that are at least 90 days old and unused for at least 90 days. SQL WITH latest_reports AS ( SELECT _cq_platform_id, arn, `user` AS principal, access_key1_active, access_key_1_last_rotated, access_key_1_last_used_date, access_key2_active, access_key_2_last_rotated, access_key_2_last_used_date FROM aws_iam_credential_reports ORDER BY _cq_sync_group_id DESC, _cq_sync_time DESC LIMIT 1 BY _cq_platform_id ), keys AS ( SELECT _cq_platform_id, arn, principal, 1 AS key_slot, access_key1_active AS active, access_key_1_last_rotated AS created, access_key_1_last_used_date AS last_used FROM latest_reports UNION ALL SELECT _cq_platform_id, arn, principal, 2 AS key_slot, access_key2_active AS active, access_key_2_last_rotated AS created, access_key_2_last_used_date AS last_used FROM latest_reports ) SELECT _cq_platform_id, arn, principal, key_slot, created, last_used FROM keys WHERE principal != '<root_account>' AND active = true AND created < now() - INTERVAL 90 DAY AND ( last_used IS NULL OR last_used < now() - INTERVAL 90 DAY ) ORDER BY last_used NULLS FIRST, principal,…

articles.title: It costs a lot more to use AI models in some languages
articles.content: A new study from the Coalition for Language Equity in AI Research shows that AI models require significantly more tokens to process certain languages than others. These differences mean that users of underrepresented languages risk paying more for the same services, reports Rest of World . An LLM’s tokenizer breaks text down into blocks, or tokens , but it does so much more optimally for languages with abundant digitized data, the researchers explain. They found that among the 20 languages with the largest web presence, less common languages used from 1.5 to 5 times as many tokens as the same prompt in English. When the study was expanded to 200 languages, the difference increased to as much as 17 times in one of the models examined. Since most LLM providers charge by tokens used, that translates to much higher costs. In addition, more tokens mean longer response times and a smaller amount of information that’s able to fit into the AI models’ context windows. The researchers describe this as a hidden “tokenizer tax” and warn that it exacerbates digital inequality. This disparity is not limited to languages with few speakers, the researchers note . “If we sort by speakers instead of web presence, the tax lands on enormous populations: Punjabi (~200 million speakers), Bengali (~266 million), Urdu (~288 million), Burmese (~36 million), Amharic (~36 million). This means hundreds of millions of people billed at multiples of the English rate for the same intelligence,” the study says. Languages that use writing systems not as commonly found in the AI models’ training data are particularly affected. Examples include Burmese, Tibetan, Khmer, and Lao. Languages that use the Latin alphabet, on the other hand, often have an advantage, even when spoken by relatively few people. Related: CIOs grapple with subpar global genAI models

articles.title: US Marines join NATO mission in the Baltic Sea to protect undersea cables from sabotage as Russia continues to lurk
articles.content: A team of around four dozen U.S. Marines is joining a NATO-led operation in the Baltic Sea to help protect undersea internet cables and gas pipelines in the area. In a press release , the U.S. Marine Corps shared its plans to deploy a "specialized team" to support NATO's Enhanced Vigilance Activity Baltic Sentry operation. The move comes amid a backdrop of growing undersea cable interest, movements of Russia's shadow fleet , and fears of sabotage. The U.S. Marines are being sent from Marine Corps Base Camp Lejeune in North Carolina to provide "advanced expeditionary surveillance and tactical reconnaissance capabilities" to the region in support of Finnish and other NATO allies. Marines from 2nd Reconnaissance Battalion, 2nd Marine Division, and the II Marine Expeditionary Force Information Group are joining the mission. Capt. Johan Tillander, Chief of Operations for the Finnish Navy, explained that the "experience, skills, and systems of the U.S. Marine Corps are perfectly suited" for the operation, including "monitoring of the Baltic Sea." While the press release stresses that the Marines are serving in a "supportive, enabling capacity," with European nations taking the lead, the Marines are there to provide "highly specialized, agile force multipliers." Maj. Gen. Daniel Shipley, Commander of U.S. Marine Corps Forces, Europe and Africa, shared that its participation shows its ability to "rapidly project specialized capabilities where they are most effective," and as a result, "ensuring we can operate seamlessly as a cohesive, lethal team to deter hybrid threats" in the area. The U.S. deployment means that the operation will be able to "leverage... unique capabilities of Reconnaissance Marines, including small Unmanned Aerial Systems and littoral sensors, to feed vital data directly" to NATO. The Baltic Sea is the frontline in potential assaults against European undersea infrastructure. Several attempts have been made to sabotage cables in the area, and two cables were cut between Finland, Sweden and Europe back in 2024 . Meanwhile, Finland's own concerns about shadow fleet operations led it to set up a dedicated maritime surveillance center earlier this year to monitor activity in the Baltic Sea. Russia isn't mentioned in the U.S. press release, but the authoritarian nation is one of Europe's biggest threats in the region, and has had worsening relations with European nations for several years, particularly since it went to war with Ukraine in 2022. Over 500 incidents of Russian fishing boats loitering near undersea cables in Europe have been seen in the last four and a half years, showing a persistence in mapping and identifying, if not directly interfering, with global data links in the area.

articles.title: SK hynix-owned Solidigm is plotting a new $45 billion flash memory factory for the US, report claims
articles.content: Solidigm, an American subsidiary of SK hynix, one of the biggest flash chip makers on the planet, is reportedly in talks with the Commerce Department over plans to invest $45 billion in a new plant to be built in the United States. But, Bloomberg reports , there's a catch — Solidigm wants to be given the go-ahead to export equipment to upgrade its existing plant in Dalian, China. The company has purportedly told officials that the upgrades would allow the Chinese plant to then help finance the cost of its U.S.-based counterpart, according to unnamed sources. It's as-yet unclear how the proposal was received, or whether the Commerce Department is inclined to agree to the deal. Go deeper with TH Premium: Memory (Image credit: SK Hynix) AI data centers are swallowing the world's memory and storage supply Samsung debuts three next-generation memory technologies for AI data centers The future of DRAM: From DDR5 to future ICs High-bandwidth memory roadmap Inside the history of DRAM price-fixing lawsuits The U.S. government has been keen to drive at-home manufacturing wherever possible, including for chips used in its computers and data centers. National security is regularly cited as a key reason behind the move. It's also the reason for the government's stance on exporting technologies to China, including the equipment that Solidigm says will help upgrade its Dalian plant. Similar export restrictions are in place for high-end AI data center components, with a black market having sprung up to take the place of sanctioned sales. Earlier this month, it was reported that some of Nvidia's powerful Blackwell Ultra B300 GPUs are being used in China Telecom data centers , with no explanation of how they got there. A 2025 report claimed that a cool $1 billion worth of Nvidia AI chips had been smuggled into China, a figure that is sure to have increased significantly as 2026 draws to a close. In this case, Solidigm's planned Chinese factory upgrades could be mutually beneficial, allowing funds to be transferred to the new U.S. plant. But that requires the U.S. government to give it permission to ship the machinery in the first place, something that is far from guaranteed. The Dalian factory produces NAND flash memory, the likes of which are used in everything from relatively simple devices to full-blown data centers. It also comes at a time when global NAND production is a hot-button topic. Samsung and SK hynix are upgrading their Chinese factories to produce more of the chips used in AI data centers in an attempt to meet growing demand. Manufacturers have already slashed production of consumer-focused memory in favor of the more lucrative data center-grade components, causing prices to spike globally. This volatility in the market as a whole was given as one of the reasons SK hynix chose to cancel a planned Solidigm IPO earlier this week. Beyond dangling a $45 billion plant, Solidigm has also allegedly told the Commerce Department that its total investment in U.S. manufacturing could reach $100 billion eventually, with construction in New York penciled in for 2027. The company is fresh from its latest earnings call, where it announced revenues of $75 billion with $60 billion in operating profit, and $28 billion in net. The company made no mention of its Dalian plant or a planned US investment, but did warn that memory shortages are set to last through 2030.

articles.title: How Beta Technologies Is Clearing the Runway for Electric Flight
articles.content: In the cockpit of Beta Technologies’ Alia CX300, pilot Chris Caputo steers onto Runway 33 at Patrick Leahy Burlington International Airport in Vermont. Cleared for takeoff, he releases the brakes and nudges the throttle forward. At the back of the aircraft, the five-blade pusher propeller snaps awake, and the Alia bolts forward. There’s no shriek of a turbofan spooling up, no shudder of a piston engine, and no wait for thrust. Just the low hum of an electric motor and a shove of instant acceleration. Within a few seconds, we’re at 85 knots (almost 160 kilometers per hour), and Caputo rotates the nose upward. The runway drops abruptly away as we climb. Gaining speed and altitude, we head northwest over Lake Champlain. Through the wraparound canopy, I watch the hunched shoulders of Vermont’s Green Mountains shrink under the right wing, with New York’s taller Adirondacks to the left. Caputo, a former Air Force fighter pilot, flicks the control stick hard left, then right. Despite its 15-meter wingspan, the Alia feels snappy, its fly-by-wire system automatically coordinating aileron and rudder inputs. The machine, he says, is much simpler to manage than the Cessna 182 I flew around Australia in my student-pilot days. What’s more, our half-hour flight in the Alia will consume only about US $9 worth of electricity. The same flight in a comparable Cessna 208 Caravan would burn roughly 25 to 30 gallons of Jet A fuel, costing about $210 to $255 at press time. “Even at full throttle, we’re not burning any fuel up here,” says Caputo, as he takes the Alia into a sweeping left turn and heads south over the lake. “We’re not polluting the environment. [There’s] no noise pollution.” At Beta’s South Burlington, Vt., facility, workers assemble the body of an Alia A250. The company says it has an order and option-to-buy backlog of nearly 1,000 aircraft. Beta Technologies This ride is happening during an unusually lively time for electric aviation. The promise of lower operating costs and cleaner flight has pushed electric aircraft from a fringe experiment to one of the aviation industry’s most closely watched frontiers. After years of renderings, prototypes, and overly optimistic timetables, companies are now flying full-size aircraft, submitting hardware to regulators for certification, building factories, and testing routes with prospective customers. Among the top three U.S. developers of electric planes, Archer Aviation and Joby Aviation are concentrating on piloted vertical-takeoff-and-landing air taxis, otherwise known as eVTOLs. Beta Technologies is taking a broader—and in some ways more innovative—path into the market. Rather than betting first on air taxis, Beta is looking to enter electric aviation through short-haul freight planes that use conventional runways, fed by an open charging network that’s designed to make electric aircraft—both Beta’s and its competitors’—part of a working transportation system. To that end, the company is developing two variants of its Alia airframe: the runway-based CX300 I’m flying in and the A250 , which adds four lift propellers for vertical takeoff and landing. Beta says its test pilots have flown the Alia family more than 300,000 kilometers, including doing multiple U.S. crossings and overseas demonstrations. The company claims an order and option-to-buy backlog of 991 aircraft. RELATED: From Hockey Enforcer to High-Flying eVTOL CEO “We’re taking a pragmatic stepwise approach for both certification and market entry,” says Beta’s CEO and founder Kyle Clark . “We’re ready to go today with medical and cargo aircraft that fly from airport to airport.” Next up, he says, will be passenger aircraft with conventional takeoff and landing, followed by cargo eVTOLs, and finally passenger eVTOLs. Reducing the Risk of FAA Certification Beta’s 17,500-square-meter production facility sits beside the Burlington airport and looks more like a giant sunlit workshop than a conventional airplane factory. articles.title: AI agents need to be replaceable – without losing your work
articles.content: An agent receives approval to process a partial refund. It sends the request to a payment API, and the process crashes. Maybe the payment service completed the refund. Maybe the request never went through. A replacement agent spins up and finds an operation record marked dispatched with no outcome written. This kind of ambiguity isn’t unique to agents. Any distributed worker crashing mid-mutation faces the same problem. But a conventional worker resumes a predetermined workflow from the last checkpoint. An agent does something more dangerous: it reasons on its own. Given the same customer request and no outcome record, it might come up with a different plan, pick different parameters, or decide to issue a new refund instead of continuing the one already approved. “An agent does something more dangerous: it reasons on its own.” If the original refund went through, a second attempt refunds the customer twice. The charge still has enough remaining balance to cover another partial refund, so nothing stops it. The replacement must inherit the original operation, not reinterpret it. The operation must outlive the agent An agent’s process, its in-memory variables, its transient reasoning context : all disposable. The business operation is not. The refund, its approval, its parameters, its current status. A long-running agent can preserve useful state for as long as it runs. The requirement: no essential operation should depend on the original execution surviving. Before dispatching the refund, the application commits a durable operation record to a transactional store. That record includes the approved amount, the applicable authorization, the idempotency key the application sends to the payment provider, the application’s operation identifier in the provider’s metadata, and a status. “An agent’s process, its in-memory variables, its transient reasoning context: all disposable. The business operation is not.” The status moves from created to dispatched as the request leaves, and to confirmed or failed only on a provider response. If the agent crashes, the replacement retrieves this record and its correlation identifiers. A record stuck in dispatched indicates a call was attempted, but the outcome was never written. The replacement inherits the approved operation rather than regenerating it. When the replacement needs to verify the outcome, it can list refunds against the original charge and match the operation identifier in the returned metadata. But the durable record isn’t just context for the replacement. The application enforces it at the tool boundary: the dispatch layer validates every outbound request against the committed record. The agent can propose a next step, but only authorized operations with their original parameters and identity reach the provider. The model can’t redefine what was approved. ClickHouse Managed Postgres holds the business data, including the authoritative operation record that defines what the replacement is allowed to do. Native CDC replicates that data into ClickHouse. Application telemetry ships to ClickStack and agent traces to Langfuse , both configured to use the same ClickHouse service as their backend database. Because business data, application telemetry, and agent traces land in one database, tying an operation to the agent run that dispatched it and the failed HTTP call is a single-identifier query. Not a reconciliation across three tools. Two conditions. The application has to propagate that identifier. The operation ID must appear in the Postgres row, in the Langfuse trace attributes, and in the service’s log context, because nothing correlates it for you. And the replacement reads the record from Postgres, not from the replicated copy. CDC runs with seconds of latency. The authoritative row is the one the tool boundary enforces. articles.title: Airbnb’s next big bet: 1 million free nights a year for people in crisis
articles.content: Susan Bailey still vividly remembers the first time she hosted a family in need of emergency housing. It was 2017, and she had just renovated a property near her home in Colorado with the idea of adding it to her growing portfolio of Airbnb rentals. One evening, she got a call out of the blue from someone at Airbnb Open Homes, as Airbnb’s program for housing people in crisis was then known. “It was eight o’clock on a Thursday night,” Bailey says. Airbnb asked if she would be willing to welcome a refugee family from Iraq, arriving at midnight. That same year, Airbnb pointedly ran ads welcoming refugees in the face of President Trump’s ban on immigrants and refugees from majority-Muslim nations. Bailey didn’t know anything about her prospective guests, and there were still items left on her property’s renovation punch list. But she said yes. Four hours later, the family was at her door. In the years that have followed, Bailey has hosted families facing crises of all sorts and sizes, including the wildfires that have plagued communities in Colorado and California, where she also manages short-term rentals. “In many cases, in the beginning, we didn’t even know if Airbnb would fund their stays,” she says. “It was pretty scrappy.” Those scrappy days are now gone. Airbnb formalized the creation of Airbnb.org, an independent nonprofit, in 2020. Today, it’s making an even bigger commitment to the problem of emergency housing. “We were just getting a huge amount of demand,” Brian Chesky, Airbnb cofounder and CEO, says of the decision to create a new funding model for the nonprofit. This year, as Airbnb.org’s capabilities have accelerated, the organization is responding to a disaster a day. Going forward, a small portion of the revenue from every Airbnb booking—10 cents—will go toward free, temporary stays that are facilitated by Airbnb.org and its partners. [Images: Airbnb] Those dimes will add up; in 2025, the company booked 57 million stays and experiences. Over the next five years, the company plans to provide the nonprofit with $500 million through these dimes and supplementary donations. The new funding will position Airbnb.org to offer 1 million nights of emergency housing each year. It will also support the organization’s expanded mandate, which encompasses displacement due to disasters, like the war in Ukraine or hurricanes in Florida, as well as travel for medical care, safe shelter from domestic violence, and support for veterans. Guests stay for free; hosts are paid, but can discount their rates. For Chesky, the commitment to Airbnb.org is personal. After his mother was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2011, she took the train daily from Albany to New York City—a 300-mile round trip—in order to seek the best possible care. She wasn’t alone. “She met other people on the train, and they were going back and forth for medical treatment,” Chesky says. “They couldn’t afford to stay overnight. That made us realize, wow, there’s a lot of need out there.” Hurricane Sandy, in 2012, was similarly eye-opening for Chesky. When a New York City host inquired about helping people displaced by the hurricane, Airbnb started facilitating emergency stays in an ad hoc way, often via word of mouth. That initiative evolved into the establishment of Airbnb.org six years ago. To date, Airbnb.org has provided free stays to 250,000 people. Brian Chesky [Photo: Airbnb] The time is right to do more, Chesky says. “We’re not going to house everyone, but we felt like we finally got to the place where we had the operational capacity to make a giant commitment,” he says. “This commitment’s a five-year commitment, but we’re going to do this for a lot longer than five years. We hope to do this for as long as Airbnb exists.” Responding to the Los Angeles Wildfires The wildfires that ravaged Los Angeles County last year have become a model for how Airbnb.org operates in the face of crisis. They also underscore the hostility between Airbnb and many local…

articles.title: The Download: dead startups fueling AI and interspecies communication
articles.content: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. AI labs are buying data from dead startups to train their models When Keelan Miskell began winding down his crypto startup, he didn’t think its data was worth much. But he’s since turned the company’s digital archives into tens of thousands of dollars, selling its codebase and workspace data. He’s part of a growing market in which companies that help shut down startups sell their data to AI labs. Demand has grown as training labs hit the limits of public and synthetic datasets, with buyers seeking real-world records to help train AI agents. But the sales raise legal and ethical questions. Read the full story on the AI labs buying up the remains of failed startups . —Matthew King Are we there yet? Interspecies communication Humans are far from the only species with a gift for gab, and our furry, feathered, and finned friends could have a lot to tell us. Decoding how animals communicate with one another could reveal the inner lives of other species—and give humans a window onto how they see the world. A growing arsenal of devices and advances in AI have made it easier to study their howls, squeaks, and clicks, but making sense of it all remains complex. Find out how close we are to interspecies communication . —Cassandra Willyard This story is part of “Are we there yet?” , our series that takes stock of six technologies that have long promised to change the world—and scores them on a progress meter. We’re exploring each one in The Download, so stay tuned, and subscribe to read the rest of the stories in our new Impossible issue . But the moon is a tremendously hostile place to set up camp. A sprawling lunar base must be safe for its inhabitants, protected from falling asteroids, endless cosmic radiation, razor-sharp lunar dust, and torturous temperature swings. It also must be somewhat self-sustaining. That will require autonomous robots, nuclear power, and a way to use the moon’s resources to keep the base operating. But the chief obstacle may be one of political will . This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts . articles.title: Exclusive: Numeracle Raises $28M To Keep Legitimate Business Calls From Spam Label
articles.content: Numeracle has raised $28 million from Edison Partners to help businesses whose calls are incorrectly labeled as spam or blocked by phone carriers, it tells Crunchbase News exclusively. The McLean, Virginia-based company verifies businesses and links their identities to the phone numbers they use to contact customers. It shares that information with the systems carriers use to screen calls and works to remove incorrect labels. Rebekah Johnson, founder and CEO of Numericle. (Courtesy photo) The financing brings Numeracle’s total funding to $34.8 million since its 2018 inception. That total includes a $6.8 million Series A raised in December 2023, founder and CEO Rebekah Johnson told Crunchbase News in an interview. Edison was the sole investor in the new round. Numeracle declined to disclose its valuation. The company says it has roughly 4,000 business customers and about 85 employees. It became profitable this year, sooner than Johnson had expected. Numeracle plans to use its new capital to hire and expand internationally. The company also plans to adapt its business verification tools for use beyond phone calls. For example, Johnson said the company is eyeing messaging, chat apps, marketplaces and AI agents. Its expansion comes as businesses simultaneously face two related problems. For one, fraudsters are increasingly impersonating them. Meanwhile, call-screening systems can prevent their own calls from reaching customers. For example, that could mean a patient ignoring a call from a hospital about an upcoming procedure. For a bank, it could mean a customer declining a legitimate call because the phone displays a fraud warning. Numeracle charges an annual subscription to monitor and address incorrect spam labels. Customers can also pay a per-call fee to display their business name, logo and reason for calling on a recipient’s phone. From a regulatory warning to a company Johnson, an engineer who previously worked in regulatory compliance at telecom provider West , said she recognized the problem while participating in the Federal Communications Commission ’s Robocall Strike Force in 2016. She warned carriers that their efforts to identify unwanted calls would also affect legitimate businesses because the screening systems lacked information about who was calling. About three months later, she said, a carrier’s federal regulatory counsel called her while she was in her parents’ kitchen. “Everything you said was going to happen is happening. What do we do?” she recalled him asking. Johnson said that conversation prompted her to start Numeracle. She was a newly single mother who had lost her job and used her life savings to start the business. Living on a farm in Grand Bay, Alabama, without internet access, she worked from cafes. “When you need to feed your children and provide a roof over their head, you’re going to count every penny,” Johnson said. That experience shaped her spending decisions as Numeracle grew, she said. The company operated for several years before raising its Series A. Johnson said about 90% of Numeracle’s sales inquiries come through unpaid inbound channels. With the new funding, she plans to spend more on marketing to specific industries, including healthcare. The company’s customers also include businesses in financial services, home services and higher education, as well as government organizations and charities. Johnson declined to identify individual customers. Verifying increasingly convincing fakes Numeracle first checks that a business is real and does what it claims. Once it passes those checks, the company links it to the phone numbers it uses and shares that information with the systems carriers use to flag or block calls. Other companies can also pay Numeracle to run those checks on businesses they’re considering taking on as customers. A business call from Numeracle, delivered with name, logo, and reason for calling. articles.title: From human clicks to agentic velocity: What OpenAI’s 1.2 billion scale means for your auth
articles.content: When OpenAI announced at DevDay that ChatGPT had crossed 1.2 billion weekly active users (WAUs), roughly 15% of the human population, most engineering discussions naturally centered on model context windows, compute clusters, and distributed GPU inference . However, behind every chat session, API call, and model invocation sits an equally monumental infrastructure challenge: Identity and Access Management (IAM) at extreme web scale. “Behind every chat session, API call, and model invocation sits an equally monumental infrastructure challenge: Identity and Access Management (IAM) at extreme web scale.” Before OpenAI can serve a token from an LLM, its backend systems must authenticate the request, validate OAuth2 access tokens, inspect fine-grained permissions, and maintain secure session contexts globally. To manage this massive transaction volume without introducing latency bottlenecks, OpenAI turned to Ory , utilizing its lightweight, decoupled authentication engine and OAuth2/OIDC infrastructure. Here is an architectural breakdown of how identity scale shifts when moving from human traffic to agent workloads, why legacy IAM platforms break at this volume, and how decoupled, edge-ready authorization handles extreme throughput. The scale problem: human traffic vs. agentic workloads To understand why traditional IAM platforms fail at extreme scale, consider how user authentication patterns change as architectures evolve from standard web applications to agentic AI platforms . “When an enterprise moves from human-initiated UI clicks to autonomous AI agents… the ratio of token validations to human interactions scales non-linearly.” When an enterprise moves from human-initiated UI clicks to autonomous AI agents (e.g., OpenAI’s Work and Codex suites), the ratio of token validations to human interactions scales non-linearly: Transaction velocity: A single user request to an AI agent can trigger dozens of downstream sub-tasks, database queries, and third-party API tool calls. Each step requires session verification and token introspection. Token introspection overhead: Legacy central identity providers (IdPs) typically validate access tokens via centralized RPCs or database lookups. At billions of requests per minute, centralized introspection introduces severe network hops and database lock contention. Stateless edge verification: To prevent authorization from becoming the primary bottleneck in the request path, session validation must happen synchronously at the edge using lightweight cryptographic verification (such as JSON Web Key Sets / JWKS caching) rather than stateful network calls. Architectural comparison: modern composable IAM vs. legacy monolithic SaaS When evaluating identity platforms for ultra-high throughput, engineering teams frequently hit performance and cost walls with traditional multi-tenant identity SaaS products (e.g., Auth0, Okta, Ping Identity). Architectural dimension Legacy monolithic identity SaaS Self-hosted composable IAM (e.g., Ory) Token validation mechanism Centralized IdP round-trips or heavy server-side SDKs Edge-native stateless JWT validation & local session caching Data residency & ownership User store hosted in vendor-managed SaaS clouds Complete data sovereignty (runs directly in your VPC / multi-cloud k8s) Database persistence strategy Proprietary SaaS database clusters subject to vendor rate limits Highly available distributed SQL layers (e.g., CockroachDB, Spanner, Postgres) Cost scaling model Per Monthly Active User (MAU) or per-API request execution fees Infrastructure-based scaling; cost correlates with compute/memory footprint Customizability & velocity Restricted to vendor webhooks, rules, or custom code sandboxes Go-native microservices with clean API boundaries and headless UI integration “OpenAI wanted a partner that could help enable our vision for owning our identity processes, data, and success. We have a lot of partners, and Ory is one of our best.” Benjamin Billings,…

articles.title: The Invisible Graph: How Companies Grow Revenue And Still Lose Value
articles.content: I got off the phone with a potential client whose company is doing great. The client, however, is not even thinking of selling the company as they see future growth over the next couple of years that they wish to materialize in order to get a larger exit. The conversation prompted me to consider something I believe many entrepreneurs miss, and it’s this: Revenue can rise while enterprise value falls. When revenue and value move in opposite directions Founders and boards routinely track revenue and profitability over time. But another graph deserves equal attention: enterprise value. Its trajectory can turn downward while the operating numbers continue improving, with significant implications for M&A timing. Consider a hypothetical SaaS company generating $15 million in annual recurring revenue, valued at 6x ARR. Its implied enterprise value is $90 million. Two years later, ARR reaches $20 million, but the multiple falls to 3.5x revenue. Enterprise value drops to $70 million. Revenue increased 33%, while value declined 22%. These are only illustrative assumptions to demonstrate how multiple compression can overshadow operating growth. For a founder postponing a sale until the next revenue milestone, the practical implication is clear: Reaching that milestone may still produce a smaller exit. Qualitative, absolute and relative factors The revenue multiplier reflects several dimensions that evolve differently. Qualitative factors include management quality, founder dependence, competitive intensity, product differentiation and strategic relevance to buyers. Absolute financial measures include revenue, EBITDA and cash flow. Relative performance measures include growth, margins, net revenue retention and gross revenue retention. Although retention metrics are expressed as percentages, their importance lies in what they reveal about customer durability and expansion. Buyers assess these measures together and compare them with relevant peers. As companies mature, their absolute results can improve while their growth rates weaken. Meanwhile, stronger profitability, better retention or deeper management capabilities may support a higher multiplier. The valuation outcome depends on the combined effect. Boards should therefore ask which characteristics will improve over the next year, which could deteriorate and how buyers might price those changes. M&A preparation should begin while you are winning A sale requires preparation, buyer engagement, negotiation and diligence, during which buyers continually reassess performance and forecasts. Waiting until a slowdown becomes visible can weaken negotiating leverage and raise questions about management’s projections. Strategic buyer demand also follows its own timetable. A buyer may place substantial value on acquiring a particular technology, customer base or geographic presence today. That interest can diminish after an internal product launch, a competing acquisition or a budget change. Waiting can still create considerable value when additional scale attracts more buyers, profitability improves or concentration falls. Boards can make that case tangible by reviewing estimated enterprise value alongside the operating plan, using scenarios in which revenue grows while the multiple holds, expands or contracts. They should also consider how debt, cash, dilution, liquidation preferences and transaction terms affect shareholder proceeds. Nobody can reliably identify the valuation peak in advance. However, every decision to delay a sale embeds a view about future valuation. That view deserves its own graph. Itay Sagie , a guest contributor to Crunchbase News, is a seasoned lecturer and strategic adviser to startups and investors, specializing in strategy, growth and M&A. You can connect with him on LinkedIn for further insights and discussions. Related Crunchbase query: Global M&A In 2026 For Venture-Backed Companies Illustration: Dom Guzman

articles.title: Trump says Microsoft abuses visa laws. Microsoft disagrees. Who’s telling the truth?
articles.content: Decades ago, the United States established programs that allow businesses to hire highly skilled foreign workers — the H-1B visa program and a related green card program. They’re designed to make sure we lead the world in technology. Not uncommonly, H-1B workers and green card holders eventually become American citizens. One of the best-known examples is Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella. He came to the US from India on the green card program, then switched to the H-1B visa program in the early to mid-1990s when working for Microsoft. He ended up becoming a US citizen. In 2014, he was appointed Microsoft CEO and subsequently architected one of the biggest turnarounds in tech history. Under his leadership, Microsoft has become nearly a $4 trillion company. President Trump, who rode an anti-immigrant message to the White House two times, has both the green card and H-1B programs in his crosshairs — and he’s aiming right at Microsoft. Earlier this month he claimed Microsoft, Adobe, and several other companies had abused an important part of the green card program called PERM, which helps H-1B visa holders get green cards. He’s suspended their use of it . Microsoft fired back that Trump was off target and the company has done nothing wrong. Who’s right and who’s wrong? We’ll follow the facts to find out. Trump’s and Vance’s fact-free charges against Microsoft A green card allows a foreigner to stay and work in the US permanently. Companies often sponsor people for green cards, although there are other ways someone can get one as well. Once someone has a green card, they can switch to work for a company other than the one that sponsored them. Getting a green card is often a first step for someone to become a US citizen. An H-1B visa, on the other hand, is temporary and allows a skilled worker to stay in the US for three years, which can be extended to six years. The two programs are closely related. Not uncommonly, someone on an H-1B visa can get a green card by having the company sponsoring them apply for it through the PERM program. PERM is what Trump targeted earlier this month. He suspended Microsoft, Adobe, and several other companies from the PERM program so they can’t get their H-1B workers green cards. Vice President Vance claimed Microsoft had “abused” the system by laying off American workers and replacing them with lower-cost foreign workers. He said in a news conference that there was “no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused this system more.” Vance contends that Microsoft laid off 6,000 American workers in the past year and replaced them with much less expensive foreign H-1B visa and green card holders. He called the foreign workers “indentured servants.” Vance concluded, “If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants. Now that is a scandalous system.” That’s pretty damning, if true. But as so often is true with the Trump administration, the charges bear no relationship to the truth. For one thing, Vance’s numbers include Microsoft’s use of the H-1B program as well as the green card program. It’s not just PERM and the green-card program that Trump has been attacking. Since his first election, he’s targeted the H-1B visa program as part of his war on immigrants and immigration. Last year, he imposed a $100,000 fee on companies for each H-1B visa they use, a move which a judge earlier this year ruled was illegal . His administration has appealed the ruling. In August, the Department of Homeland Security proposed a similar fee plan, with companies having to pay $103,265 to hire an H-1B worker . The administration has also filed proposals to end work authorization for some H-1B workers’ spouses and eliminate the 60-day grace period H-1B workers have now to stay in the US after a job loss so they can look for new work. articles.title: From Monk To Startups: One Founder’s Unusual Path To Building Government Software
articles.content: Editor’s note: The following is the latest profile in a series of articles about startup founders from non-technical backgrounds who have launched successful venture-backed companies. Read the previous interviews in the series including with MagicSchool AI founder Adeel Khan here , Trunk Tools founder Sarah Buchner here , Tabs founder Ali Hussain here , Craft founder Ilya Levtov here , GC AI founder Cecilia Ziniti here , Incredible Health co-founder Iman Abuzeid here , and Hilt founder William “Will” Cielen here . Lilly Chen was 16 and had been repeatedly hospitalized for Graves’ disease when her mother suggested they move to China and become monks. Frustrated with the care her daughter was receiving through Medicaid, she wanted to try something different. Lilly Chen, co-founder and CEO of FSH Technologies. (Courtesy photo) Chen left high school and spent about two years as a monk, ordained in the United States before spending several months at a monastery in China. She meditated, reread the same books, and gradually felt well enough to consider returning to school. She went on to enter Colorado College without a high school diploma, briefly play video games professionally, and become an engineer at Facebook . When she quit that job, she didn’t have a startup idea. She just wanted to find work she believed in. That mission eventually led her to FSH (pronounced “fish) Technologies ,” a Philadelphia-based company that’s building software for some of the government’s least glamorous tasks, including administering school food services and managing public records. After her brief stint at a large tech company, Chen realized she wanted to tackle the everyday problems that make people’s lives harder, even if solving them wouldn’t generate much excitement in Silicon Valley. “What does it actually take to solve the really unsexy, boring stuff?” she remembers asking herself. A different route to college Before Chen was thinking about government software, she was trying to get well enough to return to school. At the monastery in China, she meditated, ate food grown on-site or brought by nearby villagers, and lived without internet access. She continued taking thyroid medication and said her health became more manageable during that period. She also read. A lot. With no nearby place to buy books, she reread the ones she had brought, finding different places around the monastery to sit with them. Her attachment to those books prompted a conversation with a fellow monk who asked what she enjoyed about reading and where she might find more books. The discussion eventually turned to colleges, and why she wasn’t attending one. Chen explained her health problems. He observed that she seemed well. She realized she was. So Chen returned to the U.S., homeschooled herself and enrolled at Colorado College without having earned a high school diploma. She turned 20 during her freshman year and graduated in 2019 with a double major in mathematics and economics. While she was in college, Chen briefly played Dota 2 professionally. She also played against OpenAI ’s game-playing bots, an early encounter with AI technology she would later help support as an engineer. After an initial job in Boston, she joined Facebook, where she built infrastructure used to train AI models. Leaving without a startup idea Then on Jan. 6, 2021, Chen was attending a remote company all-hands meeting while watching coverage of the attack on the U.S. Capitol on another screen. Her concerns about Facebook’s role in enabling the organization of violence made her question whether she could continue working there. “I realized that I couldn’t work for Big Tech anymore,” she recalls. She quit shortly afterward. To figure out her next move, she returned to the sort of questions she had encountered as a monk. What made her happy? What mattered to her? What was she good at? Programming remained her most concrete skill. She just needed to figure out where to apply it. An introduction…

articles.summaryEn: Lilly Chen, co-founder and CEO of FSH Technologies, became a monk at 16 after struggling with health issues. After a brief stint as an engineer at Facebook, she founded a startup focused on solving mundane government problems, despite the lack of excitement in Silicon Valley.
insightsFa: لی لی چن تجربه منحصربه‌فردی از زندگی راهبی تا کارآفرینی دارد.
